prompt: A public hospital wants a new scheduling system. Its budget and go-live date are fixed by the annual budget law, but nobody can yet say which screens the wards will need. Which contract fits that situation best?
hint: Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 1.

choices.text: Fixed price, with the scope, cost and date all written into the bid
choices.why: It fixes the one thing nobody knows yet, the scope, and turns every later discovery into a negotiation.

choices.text: Time and materials, paying for whatever effort the work needs
choices.why: The budget here is fixed by law, and time and materials leaves the client carrying an uncertainty it cannot pay for.

choices.text: Fixed budget and date, with the scope left open to agree as the work goes
choices.why: This is fixed-price, variable-scope: it writes the agile bet into a legal document, keeping the two fixed things fixed and the unknown one open.

choices.text: A first contract for the requirements phase alone, then a fixed bid on the rest
choices.why: It still freezes the scope early, at the wide end of the cone of uncertainty, before any ward has tried a screen.

prompt: On day 4 of a ten-day Sprint, the Developers find that one of the five items behind the Sprint Goal is twice the size they thought. What does the Scrum Guide let them do?
hint: Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 2.

choices.text: Ask the Scrum Master to extend the Sprint by the days the item needs
choices.why: A Sprint has a fixed length and the next one starts at once; nobody stretches it to fit the work.

choices.text: Cancel the Sprint and plan a new one around the larger item
choices.why: Only the Product Owner may cancel a Sprint, and only when its goal has become obsolete, which a big item does not do.

choices.text: Keep all five items and work late, because the Sprint Backlog is a promise
choices.why: The commitment is the goal, not the list; a team that can only succeed by finishing every item has a to-do list.

choices.text: Renegotiate the Sprint's scope with the Product Owner and keep the goal
choices.why: The Sprint Goal exists to give that room: the Developers and the Product Owner may trade items and still succeed.

prompt: Halfway through a Sprint, two items are added to the Sprint Backlog, and the burndown simply falls more slowly. Which chart would have shown the added scope as a line of its own?
hint: Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 2.

choices.text: A burn-up, plotting work done against a separate line for the total
choices.why: A burn-up draws completed work and total scope as two lines, so added scope shows up as the top line rising.

choices.text: The burndown's ideal line, redrawn every day from the new total
choices.why: The ideal line runs once from the committed total to zero; redrawing it would hide the change rather than show it.

choices.text: A velocity chart, with one bar for each of the last eight Sprints
choices.why: Velocity counts the points finished per Sprint; it says nothing about what happened inside this one.

choices.text: The cycle-time scatter, one dot for each item that finished
choices.why: The scatter shows how long finished items took; scope that has not finished is not on it at all.

prompt: The Agenda team is sorting rules into its Definition of Done and into the acceptance criteria of single items. Which belong in the Definition of Done? Choose all that apply.
hint: Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 2.

choices.text: Every change keeps the booking screen's p95 response time under the agreed limit
choices.why: A quality rule every change must keep is a non-functional requirement, and the Definition of Done is where it gets teeth.

choices.text: The whole automated test suite passes
choices.why: It applies to every item and can be checked with a yes or a no.

choices.text: The change is deployed to staging and checked there
choices.why: How finished an item must be is the same for every item, so it is a line of the Definition of Done.

choices.text: A patient can cancel up to 24 hours before the appointment
choices.why: This says what one item must do, which makes it an acceptance criterion of that item.

choices.text: The code is of good quality
choices.why: Nobody can answer it with a yes or a no, so it is not a line; "the whole suite passes" is.

choices.text: The receptionist's calendar shows cancelled slots in grey
choices.why: It belongs to one story about the calendar, so it goes in that story's acceptance criteria.

prompt: A department plans the Agenda team so that every developer is allocated at exactly 100%, and asks it to start three more items now so that nobody ever waits for work. Throughput has held at about five items a week. What should the lead expect?
hint: Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 3; Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 12.

choices.text: Items finish sooner, because more of them are being worked on at once
choices.why: With the same throughput, Little's law says more work in progress means each item takes longer, not less.

choices.text: Every item takes longer, and requests queue longer as people near fully busy
choices.why: Little's law ties more work in progress at the same throughput to longer cycle times, and the queueing curve explodes as busyness nears 100%.

choices.text: Throughput rises in proportion to the work started, and cycle time holds
choices.why: Starting more work does not raise throughput by itself; it raises work in progress, and cycle time rises with it.

choices.text: Nothing changes until a WIP limit is reached, since the limits are what create queues
choices.why: Limits restrict how much is started; queues come from work piling up with no slack to absorb it, limit or not.

prompt: A team merges a three-month feature into the main line every day, hidden behind a feature flag. Its lead time for changes, from merge to production, is a few hours, and a director presents that as proof the feature was delivered fast. What is right and what is wrong here?
hint: Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 4; Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 7.

choices.text: Both are wrong: unfinished work belongs on a branch until it is complete
choices.why: A branch open for three months is exactly what continuous integration rules out; merging hidden work daily is the cure.

choices.text: Both are right, since lead time for changes measures how fast users got the feature
choices.why: The metric covers the pipeline from merge to production; with the flag off, no user had the feature at all.

choices.text: The daily merge behind a flag is good practice; reporting it as delivery is the trick
choices.why: Merging unfinished but hidden keeps integration continuous; counting those merges as the feature's delivery changes what is counted, not what users received.

choices.text: The report holds, but the flag is a risk because hidden code skips the tests
choices.why: Code behind a flag is built and tested on every merge like any other; only its release to users is held back.

prompt: The online-booking release is a month late, and a director offers four developers from another team, from Monday, to bring it back to its date. What should the lead answer?
hint: Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 5; Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 12.

choices.text: Not for this date: newcomers cost capacity first, so move scope or date
choices.why: Brooks's law and the capacity arithmetic agree: for a date next month, scope, date and confidence are the levers that work.

choices.text: Yes: four more people raise the team's capacity from their first week
choices.why: New people need training from the people already there, so they reduce the team's capacity before they add to it.

choices.text: Yes, but only on the critical path, where any added person shortens the project
choices.why: The critical path is where help could matter, but for a date next month the training and coordination still cost more than they give.

choices.text: No, because Brooks's law says a project should not grow once it has begun
choices.why: Adding people is right for a team that will exist for years and needs the capacity; the law is about late projects and short dates.

prompt: Put the parts of a SAFe PI Planning in the order the lesson gives them.
hint: Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 5.
items: Business owners present the context and the vision
Teams plan in breakouts and negotiate their dependencies face to face
Draft plans are reviewed, and management resolves what the teams could not
Teams adjust their plans on the second day
Everybody shows one to five fingers in a confidence vote
trap: Voting before management has resolved the problems the teams could not would ask people to commit to a plan with its impossible parts still in it.

prompt: A project has a budget at completion of R$ 300,000. At week 5 it has earned R$ 120,000 of work and spent R$ 150,000 to do it. Using the lesson's forecast from the cost performance index, what is the estimate at completion, in reais?
hint: Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 6.

prompt: A project has five activities, in working days. A (2) comes first. After it, B (5) and C (2) can start. D (4) needs C. E (2) needs both B and D, and comes last. The sponsor can lend one developer to cut a single activity by a day. Which choice brings the end date forward?
hint: Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 6.

choices.text: B, because at five days it is the longest single activity
choices.why: A, B, E takes 9 days and A, C, D, E takes 10, so B has a day of slack and a day saved there moves nothing.

choices.text: D, because it sits on the longest path through the network
choices.why: A, C, D and E have zero slack; a day saved on any of them, D included, is a day off the project's 10.

choices.text: Any of them, since each day cut comes off the 15 days of total work
choices.why: The longest path sets the date, not the total effort; the project takes 10 days because some work runs in parallel.

choices.text: None, since Brooks's law says one more person makes a project later
choices.why: Adding a person shortens a project when it shortens something on the critical path; Brooks says that is harder than it sounds, not impossible.

prompt: A project for a public client runs PRINCE2 Agile, with Scrum inside each stage. How does the lesson say its tolerances are set?
hint: Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 7.

choices.text: Wide on scope, and tighter on time and cost
choices.why: Scope is what agile work expects to vary, so it gets the room; time and cost are held, which is fixed date and variable scope.

choices.text: Tight on scope, so the agreed features are sure, and wide on time
choices.why: That is the sequential bet, fixing what is least known; PRINCE2 Agile does the reverse.

choices.text: Zero on all six, so the board hears about each change the teams make
choices.why: Zero tolerances turn every small deviation into an exception, and the board ends up consulted on everything.

choices.text: Wide on all six, since the teams replan every Sprint anyway
choices.why: Tolerances that wide mean the first exception arrives when the project is already lost; time and cost still need limits.

prompt: The Agenda team's SLA with the clinic network promises 99.5% availability of booking. The team now sets its own internal objective for the same service. Where should that objective sit?
hint: Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 8; Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 16.

choices.text: At exactly 99.5%, so the team answers to the number the customer signed
choices.why: An objective equal to the contract only alarms when the contract is already broken, too late to act.

choices.text: At 100%, because any minute of downtime breaks the customer's trust
choices.why: 100% forbids change and is broken by the first failure, so it stops meaning anything from the second month.

choices.text: Below 99.5%, which leaves the team room for its riskier releases
choices.why: A looser objective lets the contract break before the team's own alarm rings; room for risk comes from the budget under a stricter one.

choices.text: Above 99.5%, so the alarm rings while there is still time before the contract breaks
choices.why: Teams keep the SLO stricter than any SLA, the way the ITIL lesson checks that the layer underneath can keep the promise above it.

prompt: The booking service's error budget is spent, and the signed budget policy stops feature releases until it recovers. That afternoon, a security hole in the booking API is being exploited. How should the fix reach production?
hint: Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 8; Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 16.

choices.text: It waits with the features until the budget is positive again
choices.why: The policy stops feature work, not work: fixes and security changes go first precisely when the budget is spent.

choices.text: As a standard change, since it goes through the same automated pipeline
choices.why: A standard change is low-risk routine work approved in advance; an urgent fix to an exploited hole is not routine.

choices.text: As a normal change at the next weekly board, since the service is fragile
choices.why: A hole being exploited cannot wait for a meeting; that is the case ITIL gives its own faster route.

choices.text: As an emergency change, authorised fast and reviewed afterwards
choices.why: Closing an exploited hole is ITIL's own example of an emergency change, and the budget policy lets security changes through.

prompt: An operations director defends the weekly change advisory board: "It is why our changes so rarely fail." What did the research both lessons cite find?
hint: Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 8; Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 5.

choices.text: Such a board lowers the failure rate, at the price of somewhat longer lead times
choices.why: That is the speed-for-safety trade-off people believed in, and the research did not find it.

choices.text: External approval did not cut failures, and it slowed delivery
choices.why: Accelerate found external approval tied to worse delivery and no lower failure rate, and recommended peer review with automated tests.

choices.text: The board helps only when it meets every day instead of once a week
choices.why: Meeting more often keeps the approval far from the code; the recommendation was lightweight approval close to the work.

choices.text: Teams that deploy more often fail more, so a board earns its keep there
choices.why: The opposite: the teams that deployed most often also failed least and recovered fastest.

prompt: Match each event at the Agenda help desk to how ITIL records it.
hint: Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 8.

pairs.left: Booking stops working in one clinic at 08:10
Reminders have failed on three Mondays and nobody knows why
The cause of the Monday failure is found, and a restart restores service until the fix ships
pairs.right: a known error with its workaround

pairs.left: A new receptionist needs an account

prompt: Three independent tasks have these three-point estimates, in days: O 2, M 4, P 12; O 1, M 3, P 5; and O 4, M 6, P 14. With the lesson's method, what total should the team plan with at about the 85th percentile, in days? One decimal place.
hint: Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 9.

prompt: A colleague takes each of thirty items' own 85th-percentile estimate and adds them up, to get a total the team can be 85% confident of. Why is that total wrong?
hint: Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 9; Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 10.

choices.text: It is too short, because every estimate leaves out the waiting between steps
choices.why: Leaving out the waiting is a real fault of adding estimates, but summing 85th percentiles errs the other way: it overshoots.

choices.text: It is too short, as adding up uncertainties directly always understates them
choices.why: Adding spreads directly overstates them; that is why variances are added and the square root taken.

choices.text: It is right only if one person made all thirty estimates
choices.why: Who estimated does not change the arithmetic; the fault is in adding percentiles at all.

choices.text: Percentiles do not add, since slow and fast items partly cancel
choices.why: The spread of a total grows with the square root of the summed variances, so the 85th percentile of the total needs the distribution of totals, not a sum.

prompt: The team must forecast its first integration with a new government service, unlike anything in its history. A colleague proposes running the Monte Carlo forecast on the last six weeks of throughput. What do the two lessons suggest?
hint: Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 9; Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 10.

choices.text: Run it as proposed, because a forecast drawn from real days needs no estimate
choices.why: Drawing from real days assumes the items ahead are like the items behind, which this work is not.

choices.text: Estimate it by analogy or three points: there is no history of work like it
choices.why: For genuinely new work there is no history, so a reference class or an estimate such as a three-point range has to fill the gap.

choices.text: Run it on the team's whole history since it formed, to include more bad days
choices.why: A window must cover one policy and be recent; a longer one does not make new work comparable to old.

choices.text: Give no date until the integration has produced a few weeks of throughput
choices.why: The stakeholder needs a range now, and lesson 9's techniques give one with its assumptions written down.

prompt: A director needs online booking before the clinics' contract renewal in May. Put in order the steps of the sequence that the lesson says works.
hint: Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 9.
items: The business states the target
The team produces an estimate of the work
The estimate is compared with the target
Scope, date or resources change where the two do not fit
The team commits to what is left
trap: Starting with a figure that already says May, because that is when it is needed, renames the target an estimate: only the word changed, not the work.

prompt: The lesson's rule of thumb against the fallacy of precision: state a number with no more digits than you would ___ on.
hint: Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 10.

prompt: A pre-mortem gives four risks: a 25% chance of losing 8 days, 10% of losing 30 days, 40% of losing 5 days, and a 50% chance of saving 2 days. With the lesson's method, how many working days of contingency reserve do the three threats call for?
hint: Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 11.

prompt: In a pre-mortem, the team imagines it is some months later and the project has ___, and each person writes down privately why.
hint: Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 11.

prompt: Online booking scores low in the team's RICE sheet because its confidence is 50%: nobody knows how many patients will book online rather than by phone. Its sponsor wants it higher up. What does the lesson say is the cheapest way to move it?
hint: Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 12.

choices.text: Argue its impact up to massive, since it changes every receptionist's day
choices.why: Arguing a number up is what the confidence term exists to discount; the doubt about demand is still there.

choices.text: Score it in WSJF instead, where a hunch counts as much as a measurement
choices.why: That hides the uncertainty rather than removing it. The lesson uses both formulas to find where they disagree.

choices.text: Run a short experiment with one clinic, so confidence rests on evidence
choices.why: The low score is the formula working as intended. Evidence raises confidence, and confidence is what is holding it down.

choices.text: Label it a Must in MoSCoW, so it gets built whatever it scores
choices.why: MoSCoW agrees scope for a date and does not rank; a Must chosen to dodge a score is how every item becomes a Must.

prompt: In a survey of a clinic network's patients, "my booking confirmation arrives" comes last among the things they ask for. A product owner proposes dropping the confirmation work to pay for a reminder that tells each patient which room to go to. By the Kano model, what is wrong with the proposal?
hint: Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 12.

choices.text: The confirmation is a basic: nobody asks for it, and losing it outweighs any delighter
choices.why: Basics earn no thanks when done and intense dissatisfaction when missing, and no number of delighters makes up for one.

choices.text: Nothing: a delighter pleases out of proportion to its cost, and the confirmation earns no thanks
choices.why: Earning no thanks is the mark of a basic, not of a feature with no value; it is a precondition rather than a competitor.

choices.text: The room reminder is a reverse feature, which some patients will actively dislike
choices.why: The lesson offers that reminder as a possible delighter; reverse is an auto-play video or a forced account.

choices.text: Asked Kano's pair of questions, the confirmation would come out as a performance feature
choices.why: Being better at confirming does not satisfy in proportion; a confirmation is expected, so the pair of answers marks it a basic.

prompt: Match each backlog item to the urgency profile of its cost of delay.
hint: Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 12.

pairs.left: A checkout bug that loses sales every hour
A tax rule change that takes effect on 1 January
A database version whose support ends in two years
A report filter clinic owners would use from the day it ships

prompt: A director set a target for deployment frequency, and a month later the chart shows it doubled while the change failure rate fell. Which observations point to a change in counting rather than a real cut in batch size? Choose all that apply.
hint: Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 13; Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 7.

choices.text: Lead time for changes is exactly where it was
choices.why: A real cut in batch size shortens the wait for a deployment; a counting trick cannot reach a number measured on the changes themselves.

choices.text: Time to restore after a failure has not moved
choices.why: Smaller real batches are quicker to undo; a restore time that stayed put says the failures are the same size as before.

choices.text: The pipeline ran as often as before, while twice the deployments were counted
choices.why: A raw count that matches no event is the signature of the trick: the same runs, counted again.

choices.text: Work in progress on the board fell to half
choices.why: That is a change upstream, in how the work flows, which is what a real cut in batch size looks like.

choices.text: Each pipeline run now carries fewer changes than it used to
choices.why: Fewer changes in each real run is the batch actually getting smaller on the wire, not a change in what is counted.

prompt: A new team deployed 8 times last month, and 2 of the deployments failed. How should the lead report its change failure rate?
hint: Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 13; Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 5.

choices.text: As 25%, failed deployments divided by all of the deployments
choices.why: The arithmetic is right and the rate is fragile: one failure more or less would move it by twelve points.

choices.text: Not at all, until the team passes a DORA report's threshold
choices.why: The thresholds describe other organisations; a team learns from its own count and trend, starting now.

choices.text: As "two of eight failed": too few deploys for a rate
choices.why: Below twenty or thirty deployments, the count says honestly what a percentage says with false precision.

choices.text: As the time to restore of the two failures, which is a steadier number
choices.why: Time to restore answers a different question, and the four are read together rather than one in place of another.

prompt: Two debts each pay back in about 8 Sprints today. Nothing new is built on the first. Every new booking feature is written around the second, and its interest rose by 2 hours a Sprint over the last quarter. Which should be paid first?
hint: Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 14; Technical Strategy: Debt, Budget and Build versus Buy, lesson 5.

choices.text: The first, because a debt nobody builds on is the safest one to clear in full
choices.why: Safe to clear is not the same as worth clearing: its interest is flat, so its payback means the same next year.

choices.text: Either one, since equal paybacks are what decide the order
choices.why: The payback sheet assumes flat interest; for a growing debt its figure is the optimistic case.

choices.text: Neither, until both are measured again, as one measurement shows no trend
choices.why: The second debt has already been measured twice, and the trend is the finding: waiting costs more every Sprint.

choices.text: The growing one: every week it waits costs more than its payback figure would show
choices.why: A debt that charges more every Sprint crosses its principal sooner than the sheet says, and grows its principal too.

prompt: A small reporting job nobody changes runs on a database version whose maintainers have announced the end of security updates, and the old and new versions cannot run side by side. The lesson on technical debt warns against the big rewrite. What should the lead do?
hint: Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 14; Technical Strategy: Debt, Budget and Build versus Buy, lesson 6.

choices.text: Leave it alone: code that nobody changes charges no interest
choices.why: Its interest is risk, an unpatchable flaw with a date on it; once the ground is going away, doing nothing stops being an option.

choices.text: Rebuild the job on a supported database, keeping the old one running until the new one gives the same reports
choices.why: With the foundation ending and no piece-by-piece path, a small rewrite beside the old system is the cheapest way through.

choices.text: Apply the Boy Scout rule to it on each change until it is modern
choices.why: Nobody changes the job, so there are no changes to improve it in, and the end of support is a date, not a flow.

choices.text: Pause features for a quarter and rewrite every system that reads the reports
choices.why: That widens a forced, small move into the big rewrite lesson 14 warns about, with its second-system scope.

prompt: The Agenda team is pruning its debt register. Which entries are technical debt in the lesson's sense? Choose all that apply.
hint: Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 14.

choices.text: A test suite that fails at random and has to be re-run on every change
choices.why: It works and makes every change cost more, with a recurring cost anybody can count.

choices.text: A deployment that needs three hours of manual steps
choices.why: Every deployment pays the three hours again; that is interest.

choices.text: A pricing rule written in two modules, so each rule change is made twice
choices.why: Duplicated logic makes every change more expensive and sometimes half-made, a cost that can be named.

choices.text: Bookings saved for the wrong day when a clinic changes time zone
choices.why: The system doing something it should not is a defect, fixed as a bug because it is wrong.

choices.text: There is no reporting module yet
choices.why: A feature nobody has built is scope, decided in prioritisation like any other feature.

choices.text: A framework a newer developer would not have chosen, which costs no extra time
choices.why: With no interest to name, it is a preference about a design that works, not yet debt.

prompt: The team keeps every clinic in one database for now and means to split it at fifty clinics. The architecture decision record should write down that fifty as the ___ for repayment.
hint: Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 14.

prompt: A public tender scores each bid by the qualifications of the proposed team, and lists PRINCE2 and ITIL. Your team has neither, but has run similar projects well for years. What is a certificate for here?
hint: Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 15.

choices.text: A signal to people who filter bids without knowing your work
choices.why: Certificates matter most where somebody filters candidates without knowing the work, and a scored tender is the clearest case.

choices.text: Proof the team can run this project well
choices.why: No certificate shows that; running projects well is learned by doing it.

choices.text: Nothing, as years of experience outweigh any certificate
choices.why: To the people who already know your work, perhaps; a tender scorer does not know it and filters by what is listed.

choices.text: The method itself, which is taught only in the certified course
choices.why: The knowledge is available without the certificate; the books can be read and the guides are published.

prompt: Sofia has just become the manager of the team she worked in, and books forty-five minutes with each person to ask the same five questions. Which of them does the lesson say matters most, and is the one new managers skip?
hint: Leading People: One-to-Ones, Feedback and Hiring, lesson 1.

choices.text: If you were in my seat, what would you change first?
choices.why: It is on the list, and it points at problems, which a new manager is already hunting for.

choices.text: Is there anything you think I should know that I have not asked about?
choices.why: The catch-all at the end of the list; useful, and it does not aim at what already works.

choices.text: What is going well here that I should be careful not to break?
choices.why: A new manager arrives looking for problems and breaks what works; on Agenda this question found Diego's fast reviews.

choices.text: What do you need from me that you did not get before?
choices.why: A useful question about her own role, but the one people skip is the one about what not to break.

prompt: Renata and Diego wrote one page saying, for each shared decision, who decides, who is consulted and who is informed. Every row names exactly one person under 'decides', because a decision with two deciders is a decision with ___.
hint: Leading People: One-to-Ones, Feedback and Hiring, lesson 2.

prompt: A mentor hands over parts of a stretch assignment with a five-step ladder of sentences. Match each of her sentences to the rung of Appelo's seven levels of delegation that says the same thing.
hint: Leading People: One-to-Ones, Feedback and Hiring, lesson 3; Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 10.

pairs.left: "Do this, this way."
"Look into it and tell me what you'd do; I'll decide."
"Decide and act; tell me afterwards."
"Decide and act; you don't need to tell me."

prompt: A team is about to publish the column layout of a nightly export that a hospital's finance department will load into its accounting software. The engineer says the layout is a two-way door: 'we can change it whenever we like'. What does the lesson say about that judgement?
hint: Leading People: One-to-Ones, Feedback and Hiring, lesson 4.

choices.text: It stays two-way only until somebody else's systems depend on it; after that, undoing it breaks them
choices.why: The lesson's caveat: something gets built on a decision before anybody notices, and the door closes behind it.

choices.text: It is right, because changing a layout costs the team one release and nothing more
choices.why: That counts only the team's cost; the hospital's software is what makes the change expensive later.

choices.text: It does not matter which door it is, since every format change should go to a design review
choices.why: Treating every decision as a one-way door is exactly the slowness the 2015 letter warns about.

choices.text: A layout is a detail of style, so it belongs to whoever reviews the pull request
choices.why: Who reviews is not the question; the door is about how hard the choice is to undo once others depend on it.

prompt: In a one-to-one, Bruno tells his manager that he has been interviewing at another company and is unsure whether to stay. What goes into the shared document they both read?
hint: Leading People: One-to-Ones, Feedback and Hiring, lesson 5.

choices.text: A line saying he is interviewing elsewhere, so that the record stays honest
choices.why: Honest notes record what was decided and agreed; this one discloses something he said in confidence.

choices.text: Nothing on the interviews; at most, her private notes say they discussed growth
choices.why: The lesson's table: nothing in shared notes, and the private page records only what she needs to act on.

choices.text: An action for her to tell their director this week, so that there is time to react
choices.why: Nothing in the document goes further without telling him first, and that sentence is what makes the meeting work.

choices.text: A neutral summary of his reasons for looking, worded so that he reads it calmly
choices.why: Neutral wording does not change what the note discloses; write what you need to act on and nothing beyond.

prompt: A tech lead's monthly count of pages shows that Ana, who always says on-call is 'fine', was woken twenty times last quarter, most of them pages passed to her from other people's weeks. What does the tech lead do with the number?
hint: Leading People: One-to-Ones, Feedback and Hiring, lesson 6; Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 8.

choices.text: Accepts her answer, since asking again after she said fine would signal distrust
choices.why: 'Fine' is the correct reply to a question with no edges; asking a better question is not distrust.

choices.text: Tells her the number shows she is not coping, and moves her off the rota for a month
choices.why: A count says where pages landed, not how she is; acting on it unasked turns a prompt into a verdict.

choices.text: Asks her again, more warmly this time, how things are going on call
choices.why: A kinder tone does not give the question edges; 'how is it going' gets 'fine' however it is asked.

choices.text: Asks, in their next one-to-one, about the worst moment of her last week on call
choices.why: The count is a prompt to ask, never a conclusion, and a question bounded in time gets past 'fine'.

prompt: A director said no to a request from the team, and the manager writes the reply with the parts both courses give a no. Match each sentence of her reply to the part it is.
hint: Leading People: One-to-Ones, Feedback and Hiring, lesson 7; Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 8.

pairs.left: "You wanted to try the new deploy tool before the spring release."
pairs.right: the need, said back in their terms

pairs.left: "The release depends on the current pipeline, and changing it now puts the date at risk."
"We can try it on the internal tools service, which has no date on it."
"I'll raise it again at quarter planning, in seven weeks."

prompt: Reviewing a new engineer's pull request, a tech lead sees that a function crashes when a clinic has no time zone set. Which comment follows both the feedback habit and the review conventions the two courses teach?
hint: Leading People: One-to-Ones, Feedback and Hiring, lesson 8; Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 11.

choices.text: "This is wrong, redo it. Please check the time zone handling more carefully before asking for a review."
choices.why: It names nothing the author could check; it is the comment that opened the feedback lesson.

choices.text: "issue (blocking): line 42 assumes a time zone, so this breaks for any account without one. Could you find where the default lives?"
choices.why: It points at the line, says why it matters, labels how much, and leaves the finding to a learner.

choices.text: "Why did you assume every clinic has a time zone? We've been bitten by exactly this before."
choices.why: A 'why' about the author's choice reads as an accusation, and here the reviewer already knows the answer.

choices.text: "Change line 42 to read the default zone from settings, and add a test for a clinic without one."
choices.why: It fixes the line and skips a learner's review's second job: leaving them able to find the next one.

prompt: A manager always opens corrective feedback with a compliment and closes it with another. Which consequences does the lesson describe?
hint: Leading People: One-to-Ones, Feedback and Hiring, lesson 9.

choices.text: After a few rounds, any compliment from her is heard as the warning before a 'but'
choices.why: People learn the pattern, and her praise stops working on its own.

choices.text: The criticism lands more softly, so people act on it sooner than on a plain one
choices.why: The lesson finds the opposite: the message gets lost between the two compliments.

choices.text: People remember whichever part they wanted to hear, and forget the rest
choices.why: That is how the message gets lost: the anxious hear the criticism, the confident leave thinking it went well.

choices.text: It works as long as the praise outnumbers the criticism by about three to one
choices.why: That ratio's mathematics was withdrawn, and no ratio tells a manager how much praise to give.

choices.text: Her compliments come out vaguer than unprompted ones, and people sense it
choices.why: Praise chosen to cushion a blow is rarely real praise, and it shows.

choices.text: The praise still teaches the team what good looks like, because it is given in private
choices.why: Calibration comes from specific praise; where it is said does not make a cushion specific.

prompt: An engineer with a good record shipped a change that caused a serious incident last week, and the postmortem listed five contributing factors. His manager wants to open a performance conversation about it. What do the two courses say?
hint: Leading People: One-to-Ones, Feedback and Hiring, lesson 10; Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 15.

choices.text: It is one event with no earlier feedback, and naming him would teach the team to report incidents later
choices.why: The pattern test fails, and a postmortem that lands on a person loses the facts the next one needs.

choices.text: It is a performance conversation, because a serious incident touches what the role requires
choices.why: Touching the role is one test of three; one event with no clear feedback before it fails the other two.

choices.text: It is fair if she keeps it blameless and uses situation, behaviour and impact
choices.why: The structure does not turn one moment into a pattern, and it still names a person for the system's failure.

choices.text: It should wait until the postmortem settles the root cause, and go ahead if it was his change
choices.why: The postmortem lists contributing factors rather than one cause, and 'human error' is where analysis starts.

prompt: Caju's senior row for autonomy says 'turns an ambiguous problem into a plan other people can work from'. Which piece of work meets all three of the tests the lesson reads in that sentence?
hint: Leading People: One-to-Ones, Feedback and Hiring, lesson 11.

choices.text: She delivered, very well, the migration Diego had already broken into twelve tickets
choices.why: The problem was framed by somebody else; executing a plan well is not turning ambiguity into one.

choices.text: From a vague complaint, she found the cause and fixed it alone, in two days
choices.why: Working code is not a plan, and nobody else worked from it; two of the three tests fail.

choices.text: She turned 'invoices confuse clinics' into a sequenced plan two colleagues built from
choices.why: Ambiguous start, a plan as the output, and other people working from it: all three tests.

choices.text: From an unclear request, she wrote a careful design that only she has worked from since
choices.why: A plan only its author works from is not what the row describes; the third test fails.

prompt: A manager is writing the promotion case for Joana, who finishes fewer items than anybody on the team because she reviews, leads incidents and writes the runbooks. Which belong in a case that has to survive a panel?
hint: Leading People: One-to-Ones, Feedback and Hiring, lesson 12; Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 8.

choices.text: Reviews she gave, with dated examples of what they caught
choices.why: Contribution includes the invisible kind, and dates make it something a stranger can check.

choices.text: Her place in the team's ranking of items finished per person
choices.why: Per-person counts measure habits, and this one punishes exactly the work that makes her case.

choices.text: The incidents she led and the runbooks she wrote, with links
choices.why: Evidence with dates and links, read by somebody who knows the context, rather than a sorted number.

choices.text: Written statements from leads of other teams who saw the work
choices.why: Other voices are the part of a case nobody can dismiss as the manager's opinion.

choices.text: That she has been on the team for seven years
choices.why: Tenure is true and irrelevant; years are not on the ladder.

choices.text: A line saying she is clearly ready for the level
choices.why: 'Ready' is the conclusion the case has to reach, not evidence for it.

prompt: A manager gives an engineer her first project to lead: a change to how refunds are calculated, released to every customer at once, with the manager as the only person she can ask. By the two courses, what is wrong with the net under it?
hint: Leading People: One-to-Ones, Feedback and Hiring, lesson 13; Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 10.

choices.text: Leading a project is too big a first stretch; she should first build from somebody else's plan
choices.why: Leading a project for the first time is the lesson's own example of one new thing, a good stretch.

choices.text: Nothing, provided the manager checks the work every day and takes it back at the first sign of trouble
choices.why: Taking the work back when it feels hard is the rescue that undoes a stretch, which is meant to feel hard.

choices.text: Refund code is familiar to the team, so the project stretches her in no direction at all
choices.why: The stretch is in leading, not in the code; the flaw is who pays if it fails and whom she can ask.

choices.text: A failure would hurt the clients rather than her learning, and nobody but her boss is there to ask
choices.why: A survivable failure and somebody safe to ask who is not the manager are both part of the net.

prompt: Add up a hiring round's cost in the team's hours, the way the lesson does. The manager reviewed 48 CVs at 10 minutes each. There were 10 technical interviews of 1.5 hours each, including the write-up. Each of 5 finalists was seen by 4 interviewers for 1.5 hours, and each finalist had a 30-minute debrief with 5 people in it. How many hours of the team's time did the round cost? Answer in hours.
hint: Leading People: One-to-Ones, Feedback and Hiring, lesson 14.

prompt: A team hiring its first junior engineers wants a structured interview, and most candidates will have no past example of explaining a decision to a client. Which kind of question fits better, and what does it need most?
hint: Leading People: One-to-Ones, Feedback and Hiring, lesson 15.

choices.text: Situational questions, scored on an anchored scale, since a hypothetical answer is easy to polish
choices.why: Situational questions suit people with less experience, and they lean on the scale more than past examples do.

choices.text: Behavioural questions, since what somebody did is better evidence than what they say they would do
choices.why: The premise is right, but a candidate with no past example has nothing to describe.

choices.text: An open conversation, so that each candidate can show their strengths in their own way
choices.why: That is the unstructured interview, which predicts much less well than the structured one.

choices.text: An estimation brainteaser, since juniors have little else to be measured on yet
choices.why: A brainteaser measures practice at puzzles under observation, which the job does not ask for.

prompt: A team is hiring for a role where the person will work mostly alone, for weeks at a time, on long data migrations. By the lesson's way of choosing a format, which technical interview fits best?
hint: Leading People: One-to-Ones, Feedback and Hiring, lesson 16.

choices.text: Caju's ninety-minute pairing session, since it showed all three things its role needed
choices.why: Caju's choice followed Caju's job; working with a colleague is not what this one mostly needs.

choices.text: Live coding against the clock, since a migration that goes wrong is a test of nerve
choices.why: Of the three, live coding is the furthest from how the job is done, and it mostly measures anxiety.

choices.text: A short, paid take-home, followed by a conversation about the decisions in it
choices.why: The format follows the job; paying reduces what it measures by accident, and the talk shows understanding.

choices.text: Pairing and then a four-hour take-home, so that every format is covered at once
choices.why: Each extra stage has to earn its cost to candidates, and four unpaid hours fall hardest on some of them.

prompt: Over two hiring rounds, one interviewer's scores are higher than everybody else's for nearly every candidate, and never below 3. What does the lesson take from that?
hint: Leading People: One-to-Ones, Feedback and Hiring, lesson 17.

choices.text: Their scales differ, so a candidate's odds depend on who interviews
choices.why: It does not say he is wrong; his 3 and Helena's 3 might not mean the same thing, and the pattern shows it.

choices.text: He is a poor judge of candidates and should stop interviewing until he is retrained
choices.why: The chart shows a difference between interviewers, not which of them is right.

choices.text: Nothing yet, since scores can only be judged against how the hired people later did
choices.why: That is a third check; laying scores side by side already shows the scale drifting.

choices.text: The others are too harsh, and their scores should be raised to match his
choices.why: Nothing says his end of the scale is the right one; calibration sessions find where the wording is unclear.

prompt: A new engineer is about to join the on-call rota. Which of these do the two courses say should be in place before her first week as primary?
hint: Leading People: One-to-Ones, Feedback and Hiring, lesson 18; Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 17.

choices.text: A runbook page for every alert able to page her
choices.why: Both courses make it a rule: an alert without a page should not be able to wake anybody.

choices.text: A shadow week and then a reverse-shadow week beside an experienced engineer
choices.why: The first primary week comes after both steps, not instead of them.

choices.text: A rule that she does not pass hard pages to the expert during her first month
choices.why: Passing a hard page on is right during an incident; the fix is to make it less necessary.

choices.text: Escalation written down, saying that calling the backup at night is expected
choices.why: It answers the reason Thiago gave for staying silent: he had not wanted to wake anybody.

choices.text: Her first primary week straight after she joins, since real pages teach fastest
choices.why: In the plan, the first primary week comes after ninety days and two supervised weeks.

choices.text: A higher on-call payment for her first weeks, in place of a backup
choices.why: Paying makes a rota fair; it does not make a first shift safe, and it replaces nothing.

prompt: Put the items of Renata's list for a new hire in the order the lesson gives, from the week the offer is accepted to the first day.
hint: Leading People: One-to-Ones, Feedback and Hiring, lesson 18.
items: a message from the manager, saying what the first week will look like
laptop ordered and accounts requested
a buddy chosen and told, and the first small task written up
a short message from the buddy introducing themselves
everything working before they arrive at nine
trap: Leaving the laptop and the accounts until the last week is the usual slip, and it is how new engineers used to spend their first two days waiting; they go two weeks before, the buddy and the task one week before.

prompt: An engineer who used to finish tickets early now takes longer on every one. Her manager learns that each time she finished early she was handed the team's least wanted work. Which question of the lesson's sequence has this answered?
hint: Leading People: One-to-Ones, Feedback and Hiring, lesson 19.

choices.text: Are the expectations for this role clear to her, in words she could repeat?
choices.why: She knew what good looked like and used to deliver it; expectations are not what changed.

choices.text: Could she do it well if her life depended on it, as she used to?
choices.why: She has done it well before, so the skill is there, and something else is in the way.

choices.text: Only then, after the rest: is it a question of her motivation?
choices.why: It looks like will, and it is an earlier question in disguise, which is why motivation comes last.

choices.text: Does anything reward doing it badly, or punish doing it well?
choices.why: Finishing quickly was punished with worse work, so she learnt to finish slowly; consequences teach.

prompt: A director tells a tech lead that one engineer finishes half as many items as the rest of the team, and asks her to put him on an improvement plan. What do the two courses say she does first?
hint: Leading People: One-to-Ones, Feedback and Hiring, lesson 19; Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 8.

choices.text: Starts the plan, since items finished per person is an objective measure of output
choices.why: It measures who takes small items, and a plan before a diagnosis acts on a guess.

choices.text: Treats the count as a reason to ask, and diagnoses the cause, starting with her own part
choices.why: A per-person count shows what work landed on whom; the diagnosis finds the cause before anything is decided.

choices.text: Adds his cycle time beside the count, so that the plan rests on two numbers rather than one
choices.why: A second per-person number has the same flaw as the first; two habits do not make a contribution.

choices.text: Holds a performance conversation that names the count as the pattern he must change
choices.why: A pattern is observed behaviour after clear feedback; a count is neither, and he has had no feedback yet.

prompt: Put the five parts of an improvement plan in the order of the lesson's table.
hint: Leading People: One-to-Ones, Feedback and Hiring, lesson 20.
items: the gap, as observations with dates
the expectation, in measurable terms
the support the manager and the company will provide
the period, and when progress is reviewed
the consequences, if it is met and if it is not
trap: Opening with the expectation puts a target in front of the person before the dated facts it answers to; and the consequences go last, said plainly, rather than softened into the middle or left out.

prompt: At the end of a six-week plan, an engineer met the first half of the expectation and not the second. The pairing the plan promised for weeks one to three only began in week four, because the team was busy. What is the honest next step?
hint: Leading People: One-to-Ones, Feedback and Hiring, lesson 20.

choices.text: End the employment, since the second half of the expectation was clearly not met
choices.why: The plan failed on the company's side first, and that cannot fairly be held against him.

choices.text: Close it as met, since the half that was met shows the habit is changing
choices.why: A plan closes as met when the expectation is met; half is the partly-met case, not success.

choices.text: Say the support came late, and extend the plan once, since that gives a reason to think more time helps
choices.why: Support promised and not given voids the plan on the company's side; late support is the case an extension is for.

choices.text: Keep it open, extended week by week, until the manager feels sure either way
choices.why: An extension because the manager does not want to decide is the dishonest version in another form.

prompt: In a dismissal meeting, after the decision has been said, the engineer argues that his last late ticket was another team's fault. What does the lesson have the manager do?
hint: Leading People: One-to-Ones, Feedback and Hiring, lesson 21.

choices.text: Go back through the plan ticket by ticket, so that he leaves understanding exactly why it ended
choices.why: A long account is for the manager's comfort; the weekly summaries had already told him.

choices.text: Acknowledge it, say the decision stands and will not reopen here, and leave appeals to the people team
choices.why: Arguing implies the decision is open; if he thinks the process was unfair, the people team explains how to raise it.

choices.text: Agree to look at that ticket again with the people team, so the meeting ends fairly
choices.why: Reopening one example tells him the decision is still open, which it is not.

choices.text: Reassure him that this may turn out to be the best thing that could happen to him
choices.why: False comfort makes the manager feel better and is heard as dismissive.

prompt: Two engineers on your team are trading sharper and sharper messages in the team channel about who should set a shared queue's retry limits. Both courses would move it out of the channel. With two people who report to you, what does the lesson on conflict inside a team have you do?
hint: Leading People: One-to-Ones, Feedback and Hiring, lesson 22; Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 9.

choices.text: Reply in the thread with your own decision, so that the whole team sees it settled quickly
choices.why: A public thread is the worst place to settle it, and a mediator who decides becomes the next owner.

choices.text: Call them both into one meeting at once and have each state their case to the other
choices.why: Lívia's joint call was between two teams' leads; with two people you lead, hearing each alone comes first, since together each defends the position they arrived with.

choices.text: Take it out of the channel and ask each one alone what the disagreement about the work is
choices.why: Nobody changes position in front of an audience, and asked separately the task conflict surfaces.

choices.text: Leave it alone, since task conflict is healthy and they will reach an answer
choices.why: Task conflict also hurts once it feels personal, which this already does; resolve it quickly.

prompt: A manager argued against her director's decision to ship a payment change this week without its security review, and lost. By the two courses, what does she do?
hint: Leading People: One-to-Ones, Feedback and Hiring, lesson 22; Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 8.

choices.text: Commits: puts her disagreement on the record briefly, then does the work properly
choices.why: That is the right response to a legitimate choice she lost, and this request is not one.

choices.text: Carries it to the team as the team's decision, as with any decision from above
choices.why: Carrying decisions down applies to the ones a manager may commit to; an unsafe one is not among them.

choices.text: Ships it, but tells the team she argued against it, so they know where she stands
choices.why: It ships the unsafe change anyway, and turns the decision into something the team can resist.

choices.text: Says no plainly, in writing, and takes it to whoever the company names
choices.why: Disagree and commit covers choices between legitimate options; skipping a security review is not one.

prompt: A team began the year with 12 people and ended it with 8. Five people left during the year, and two of those departures were regretted. Using the lesson's method, what was the team's regretted attrition rate for the year? Answer as a percentage.
hint: Leading People: One-to-Ones, Feedback and Hiring, lesson 23.

prompt: An engineer resigns, saying the new job is closer to home. Her one-to-one notes show she covered two holiday on-call weeks in a row, mentioned it once and never again. What do the two courses suggest about the reason she gave?
hint: Leading People: One-to-Ones, Feedback and Hiring, lesson 23; Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 17.

choices.text: It is the safest one to give; a pager load landing on the wrong person drives people out quietly
choices.why: Nobody announces they are leaving because of the pager, and the real reasons started months earlier.

choices.text: It is the real reason, since the notes mention the on-call only once
choices.why: A theme raised once and then dropped can mean the person gave up raising it.

choices.text: Money was the likely cause, so a counter-offer would most likely have kept her
choices.why: A counter-offer works when money is the reason; the ones in her notes are still there after a raise.

choices.text: On-call load belongs to the company, since rota rules are set above the manager
choices.why: Unsustainable on-call sits with the manager first and the company second.

prompt: A director asks a manager to add a second integration this quarter, which would push back a launch the team has already promised. Which reply gives the director what a manager's manager needs and says no upwards well?
hint: Leading People: One-to-Ones, Feedback and Hiring, lesson 24; Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 8.

choices.text: Yes, then quietly moving the launch later so the team can absorb both
choices.why: A yes is a silent no to whoever loses, and the slipped launch reaches him as a surprise.

choices.text: Options with their costs, a recommendation, and 'it's your call'
choices.why: A problem with options and a recommendation can be decided quickly, and the trade-off goes to the person entitled to it.

choices.text: No, with a long explanation of why the request should not have been made
choices.why: A no is not a lecture, and with her own manager she sets out the options rather than declining.

choices.text: "We'll do our best," so he can plan while the team works out what fits
choices.why: A vague yes is the worst answer: he plans around it, and the miss arrives when nothing can be done.

prompt: In a debrief, the first opinion heard pulls everybody's later judgements towards it, even when nobody has heard new evidence. Psychologists call this effect ___.
hint: Leading People: One-to-Ones, Feedback and Hiring, lesson 17.

prompt: Asked for a promise that is not hers to give, a manager promises her own action, which can be kept, and refuses to promise somebody else's ___.
hint: Leading People: One-to-Ones, Feedback and Hiring, lesson 24.

prompt: An engineer asks her tech lead for help choosing how to grow over the next six months. Put the questions of their first conversation in the order the GROW structure gives.
hint: Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 10.
items: What would you be doing in a year that you don't do now?
What happens today when you get stuck?
What could you do to get there?
Which of those will you do, and by when?
trap: The usual slip is jumping to what she could do before the reality is clear, which is advice to an imagined person; and the choice comes last because she makes it.

prompt: On a team's cumulative flow diagram, the band between merged and deployed has grown thicker every week for a month, the development and review bands have stayed level, and the deployed line rises in steps. What is the chart saying?
hint: Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 3.

choices.text: Developers have slowed down, because trouble on a board starts in the development band
choices.why: The development band stayed level, so work leaves development as fast as it enters. The widening band is further down the board.

choices.text: Merged work is queuing for a deployment that only goes out in batches
choices.why: A widening band means work enters that state faster than it leaves, and steps instead of a slope mean the boundary is crossed in batches: changes are waiting for a release train.

choices.text: Nothing is finishing, because the lowest line on the chart has gone flat
choices.why: A flat bottom line would mean nothing finishes. A line that rises in steps is finishing, in batches.

choices.text: The backlog is growing faster than the team starts work, so promises pile up
choices.why: The backlog is the top band, between arrived and started. The band that widened here is the last one.

prompt: A team runs a Kanban board with a limit of one item per developer. When Lúcia's item is blocked by another team, the team's rule lets her start a new one, because blocked items do not count. Six weeks later the blocked item is still there and nobody mentions it. What rule does the course give instead?
hint: Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 4; Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 3.

choices.text: Move blocked items to a separate list, so the board shows the work that can move
choices.why: That is how BIL-189 disappeared: off the board it stops ageing where anybody looks and stops counting as work in progress.

choices.text: Raise the limit to two per developer, so that a block leaves nobody idle
choices.why: A limit that leaves people idle for days is too tight, but this one did not: she had work. Raising it only widens the door the block walked through.

choices.text: Leave it out of the limit, and have its developer report it at every standup
choices.why: A standup that goes round the people hears what each is working on, and nobody is working on the blocked item. That is the blind spot that hid it.

choices.text: Count it against the limit, so the place it holds makes unblocking everybody's job
choices.why: If a blocked item holds a place the team needs, the pressure to unblock it is on the whole team, and that pressure is the point of the limit.

prompt: A team's dashboard shows a median lead time for changes of six hours. A shop owner complains that a bug she reported took five weeks to reach her. Both are true. Which measurement should sit beside the DORA numbers so the report sees what she saw?
hint: Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 6.

choices.text: Time to restore, since a bug that reached a customer is a failure the team had to fix
choices.why: Time to restore covers failed deployments. Her bug was not one: it waited, and with six hours from commit to production, nearly all of the five weeks came before the first commit.

choices.text: Deployment frequency per week, since fixes reach customers sooner when releases are frequent
choices.why: Frequency counts deployments and says nothing about how long a request waited before anybody started it, which is where a five-week wait behind a six-hour lead time for changes must be.

choices.text: Lead time from the request entering the backlog to the change in production
choices.why: Lead time for changes starts at a commit, so the backlog wait is invisible to it. The requester's clock starts when the request is written down.

choices.text: Lead time for changes measured from the first commit instead of the merge
choices.why: Measuring from the first commit adds development and review, and still starts after the request has waited in the backlog for weeks.

prompt: Opening the raw list of deployments, a tech lead finds that one engineer started deploying each service separately, at the same minute, the week after the director began ranking teams by deployment frequency. By the lesson, what does she do first?
hint: Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 7.

choices.text: Fix the incentive and log the definition, before talking about the person
choices.why: The engineer answered the question somebody asked. Change the question and write the definition down, and the trick stops being worth doing.

choices.text: Raise it at his next performance review, so the team can see that it is taken seriously
choices.why: Treating it as misconduct teaches everybody to hide the next one better, which is the opposite of a generative culture.

choices.text: Recompute the quarter under the old definition, and leave the ranking where it is
choices.why: A corrected chart under the same incentive invites the next honest-looking move; the ranking is what made it worth doing.

choices.text: Forbid separate service deployments, since they inflate the count every time they happen
choices.why: Deploying services separately can be real and useful; what needs fixing is the definition and the reward, not the practice.

prompt: A team that forecasts by counting items is asked how long a migration to a new payment provider will take. It has never done a migration, and its throughput history is all feature work. What does the course recommend?
hint: Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 9; Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 9.

choices.text: Count the migration's items and run the usual Monte Carlo over the team's daily throughput
choices.why: Counting assumes the coming items look like the past ones. Work unlike anything in the team's history has no history to count.

choices.text: Hold planning poker on every migration item and add up the points into a total
choices.why: Summed points forecast no better than a count, and a sum of guesses about unfamiliar work inherits the planning fallacy.

choices.text: Find similar migrations, here or in other teams, and start from how long they took
choices.why: This is the outside view, or reference class forecasting: the past projects' durations already contain the delays that imagining the plan leaves out.

choices.text: Decline to give a date, in the spirit of #NoEstimates, and report progress as it comes
choices.why: #NoEstimates is not a refusal to say when. And new work is exactly the case the course keeps estimation for.

prompt: For thirty items left, one colleague proposes three-point estimates per item, PERT means added up and variances combined to get an 85th percentile. The tech lead prefers a Monte Carlo forecast from the team's daily throughput. What does the throughput forecast take into account that the summed estimates leave out?
hint: Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 10; Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 9.

choices.text: The spread of each item, which the PERT arithmetic has no correct way to combine
choices.why: PERT does combine it: variances add when the tasks are independent. The gap is in what each estimate describes, not in how they are added.

choices.text: The waiting, the parallel work and the interruptions already inside each day's count
choices.why: An estimate describes the work on an item. A day's throughput is what the team actually finished, with every queue and interruption included, so a forecast drawn from it does not need anybody to imagine them.

choices.text: A single date the stakeholder can plan around, instead of a range to argue over each week
choices.why: A Monte Carlo forecast is a distribution, read at several percentiles. It replaces a single date with a range, not the other way round.

choices.text: The size of each item, which a plain count of items necessarily throws away
choices.why: The simulation counts items and ignores their size, which is why it needs items of broadly similar size. Size is what it does not use.

prompt: Marta wants all thirty items of the invoicing screen by the 6 November fair, which the forecast calls a coin toss, and adds: "Surely the team can skip the load test and the 5% release, just this once?" What should Bia answer?
hint: Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 11; Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 13.

choices.text: Ask for two engineers from another team for the month, so the date holds with testing
choices.why: Adding people to a late plan takes capacity before it adds any: newcomers need explaining, reviewing and coordinating. It is the reflex both courses warn against.

choices.text: Say yes to the date to end the argument, and let the team absorb it in evenings
choices.why: That moves the risk from the person who can manage it to a team that cannot, and it is paid for in evenings and in the next forecast.

choices.text: Quote mid-November as the date, and keep the end of October to herself as a buffer
choices.why: A secret buffer is padding. It is found out the first time the team finishes early, and every later forecast is discounted.

choices.text: Keep the testing, and let Marta fix two of scope, date and confidence
choices.why: Quality only looks like a lever because nobody sees it move until January. The honest trade is between the other things: fewer items, a later date, or the date with its risk and a fallback agreed now.

prompt: A director tells the team: "Write 6 November down as the estimate, because that is when the fair is." What has just happened, in the terms both courses use?
hint: Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 11; Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 9.

choices.text: A target has been renamed an estimate; the team should answer with its forecast range
choices.why: The fair is what the business wants, a target. An estimate is a prediction about the work, and only after comparing the two can anybody commit to something.

choices.text: A commitment has been made, and the team now owns the date whatever happens
choices.why: Nobody compared the date with the work, so nothing has been committed. Treating it as a commitment leaves the risk with the team, silently.

choices.text: A sound estimate has been given, since a date fixed by the outside world is firm information
choices.why: A fixed date is real information about the business. It says nothing about how long the work takes, which is what an estimate predicts.

choices.text: A buffer has been added, because a fair date is safer than a date from history
choices.why: Nothing was padded; the date came from the calendar, not from the work. Padding would be a deliberate margin on top of a forecast.

prompt: At 23:40 a SEV2 is declared on card charges. Three people are awake: Rafa, who wrote most of the card code, Caio and Inês. Rafa says: "I'll fix it and post the updates myself, it's quicker." Which arrangement do the two courses point to?
hint: Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 13; Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 14.

choices.text: Rafa takes command, since the person who knows the system best should decide
choices.why: The person who knows the system best is needed at the keyboard as technical lead. A commander who opens a terminal leaves nobody coordinating.

choices.text: Rafa holds every role, since a small incident lets one person hold them together
choices.why: One person may hold all four in a small SEV3. In a SEV2 with three people awake, the updates would stop at the hardest moment.

choices.text: Rafa fixes; Inês commands; Caio writes the updates on the clock the severity sets
choices.why: The fixer and the communicator should not be the same person, or the updates stop when the problem is hardest. The commander coordinates and does not debug.

choices.text: Rafa fixes and nobody writes updates until service is back, to avoid saying anything wrong
choices.why: Updates go out on a fixed rhythm whether or not anything changed. Silence is read as nobody working on it, or as worse than they say.

prompt: At 18:10 the communications lead drafts this update for support: "We think the new retry logic is double-charging cards. Should be fixed in 15 minutes." What should change before it goes out?
hint: Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 13; Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 14.

choices.text: Nothing; support needs the cause, or it has nothing to tell the shops
choices.why: Support needs a true sentence to say to the next caller, not an explanation. A guessed cause becomes, an hour later, what the shops were told.

choices.text: Drop the guess and the promise; say the impact, what is being done, and the next update time
choices.why: A cause belongs in the postmortem until it is confirmed, and a fix time is a promise nobody can keep. A time for the next update is one the comms lead can keep.

choices.text: Add the name of the developer behind the retry, so support knows whom to ask
choices.why: Updates name no one. A name in a message to support becomes blame by the evening, and it sends questions to the people fixing.

choices.text: Hold it until the fix is confirmed, so nobody has to correct a message later
choices.why: Silence during an incident reads as nobody working on it. The update goes out on its clock, thin if need be.

prompt: Marta asks for a login to the team's live ageing chart and cumulative flow diagram, so she can check them herself every Friday. What does the team's agreement on its numbers say?
hint: Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 20.

choices.text: Refuse: the working charts belong to the team, and are kept from people outside it
choices.why: The agreement keeps dashboards open to anybody who asks. Hiding them makes people find the information some other way.

choices.text: Grant it: the numbers speak for themselves, so no explanation is needed
choices.why: Read once by somebody outside, a working chart produces questions about the wrong things. The context is what makes it mean anything.

choices.text: Send her a screenshot every Friday instead, so the data is the same but frozen
choices.why: A screenshot is the same chart without the context, read the same way. It changes the format, not the misuse.

choices.text: Open them to her, and draw conclusions from them with the team in the room
choices.why: Dashboards are open to anybody who asks, and the team presents its own numbers. Conclusions drawn without it are drawn without the context.

prompt: The rollback stopped the double charges at 18:15, and the refunds will run until about 21:10. At 18:20 the head of engineering asks for the incident to be closed and "Resolved" posted. What is the right move?
hint: Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 14; Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 14.

choices.text: Downgrade it and stand people down, but keep it open until the last refund is made
choices.why: Restored is when the harm stopped; resolved is when its consequences were repaired. A downgrade fits once the harm stops; closing tells everybody, support included, there is nothing left to say.

choices.text: Close it now, since the time to restore stopped at 18:15 and that is what is reported
choices.why: Time to restore does stop at 18:15. The shops' experience does not, and closing says to support that nothing is left to tell them.

choices.text: Keep it at SEV1 with every responder on until 21:10, since shops are still affected
choices.why: Once nobody is being harmed, a SEV1 can become a SEV3 for the cleanup. Keeping everybody up for refunds costs people and buys nothing.

choices.text: Close it now and open a ticket for the refunds, which are routine work by now
choices.why: Closing at mitigation with a ticket for the rest is sometimes right; with shops still waiting for their money it hides the part they feel most.

prompt: The first draft of the postmortem timeline has the line "17:20 Rafa deployed the faulty retry release on the busiest afternoon of the month." Which rewrite do both courses ask for?
hint: Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 15; Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 15.

choices.text: "17:20 Rafa carelessly released the retry change into the month-end peak"
choices.why: This keeps the judgement and adds blame. The timeline records what happened and what people could see, and leaves evaluation to the analysis.

choices.text: "17:20 The faulty release was deployed by the team"
choices.why: Removing the name is not the point; "faulty" is. Nobody knew it was faulty at 17:20, so the word is hindsight leaking into the timeline.

choices.text: "17:20 D047 deployed, four changes including BIL-218; month-end charges running"
choices.why: It states what happened and what was true at that minute, without knowing how it ended. Where the problem lies is left for the contributing factors.

choices.text: Leave 17:20 out of the timeline, so that no person's action appears in it
choices.why: Blameless does not mean avoiding names or facts. The deployment happened at 17:20 and the timeline says so; what it must not do is stop there as an explanation.

prompt: In the postmortem meeting, a five-whys chain runs from the double charges to "the review did not ask about retries" and ends at "Duda did not think to ask". How should the team use the technique?
hint: Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 15; Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 15.

choices.text: Stop at Duda, because the chain has reached a person and that is the root cause
choices.why: Reaching a person is where the analysis begins: the next question is what made the review reasonable at the time, and the checklist did not ask.

choices.text: Ask why along each contributing factor in turn, and stop at the system each time
choices.why: Five whys follows one chain, and the chain depends on who asks. Run on every factor, it reaches the missing alert, the timing and the canary too, and each ends at something fixable.

choices.text: Drop the technique, because asking why is heard as an accusation in the meeting
choices.why: The meeting asks people how and what rather than why. That is about questioning a person, not about analysing a contributing factor on paper.

choices.text: Keep this single chain and turn its last answer into the postmortem's one action item
choices.why: One chain walks past the alert, the timing and the release to every shop. A postmortem lists every factor, then asks what makes each less likely.

prompt: A postmortem draft ends with eleven action items, every one of them a way to prevent the cause, all owned by "the team", none with a date. What should the facilitator push for before the meeting closes?
hint: Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 15; Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 15.

choices.text: Keep the eleven, since each extra fix closes one more hole in the system
choices.why: Eleven items is a list nobody finishes, and it hides the two that matter. Few items done beat many items agreed.

choices.text: Give the eleven to the tech lead, so one person answers for the whole list
choices.why: One owner per item, yes; one owner for eleven is the same list nobody finishes, with a name on it.

choices.text: Fold them into one project, a rewrite of the card code, owned by the whole team
choices.why: A single large project sits undone because nobody can start it on a Tuesday afternoon. Small actions now each close a hole on their own.

choices.text: Three to five items across prevent, detect and mitigate, each with one name and a date
