choices.why: A list that is all prevention assumes every way in was found. Few items, of more than one kind, each with an owner and a date, are the ones that get done and can be tracked.

prompt: A team with a 99.9% objective has ended each of the last five months with 85 to 90% of its error budget unused, and the shops are content. What does the lesson read in that?
hint: Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 16.

choices.text: Reliability is excellent, and the team should change nothing that produced it
choices.why: The budget is an allowance for change, agreed in advance. Leaving most of it unused month after month is value that was never delivered.

choices.text: The team is being too careful, and could ship faster or take on riskier work
choices.why: An error budget is meant to be spent. The shops would not notice a few more bad charges, and the team could have released faster or tried the risky migration.

choices.text: The objective should rise to 99.99%, since the team clearly meets it with room
choices.why: Each extra nine is ten times stricter and costs far more. It promises the shops something nobody asked for and pays for it with every release.

choices.text: The unused budget should be carried into the next month, as a reserve for a bad one
choices.why: The rolling window moves forward a day at a time, and an old good day simply leaves it. The lesson's reading is about how the team spends, not about saving.

prompt: A four-person team sets up a pager rota for every hour of the week, one week each in turn. Against the two figures from Google's SRE book that the lesson uses, how does it stand?
hint: Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 17.

choices.text: At the ceiling already, and the first holiday pushes somebody past a quarter of their time
choices.why: One week in four is exactly a quarter; one absence makes it one week in three. About eight people are what covering every hour from one place needs, with room for leave.

choices.text: Comfortable, because one week in four sits well inside the ceiling the book gives
choices.why: A quarter of a person's time is the ceiling itself, not a figure well inside it. Five people is already a rota with no margin.

choices.text: Fine, provided each person is paid a third of their hourly wage while on call
choices.why: Paying for availability makes a rota fair, not bearable or large enough. The share of time on call is the same whatever it is paid.

choices.text: Too small unless the shifts are cut to one day, so that nobody gets tired
choices.why: Shorter shifts mean more handovers, and the share of each person's time on call stays one in four whatever the shift length.

prompt: A postmortem agrees a detect action: a new paging alert when database connections pass 90%. Under the working agreement the Billing team wrote after pruning its alerts, what happens to it first?
hint: Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 18; Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 15.

choices.text: It pages from the first day, since it came out of a postmortem and has a reason
choices.why: Every alert has a reason when it is written. The rule exists so that its reason is tested on tickets before it costs anybody a night.

choices.text: It replaces the burn-rate alert, since it warns about the cause before the symptom
choices.why: The two do different jobs: a specific alert catches a failure somebody has already imagined, and the burn rate catches the ones nobody has. Neither replaces the other.

choices.text: It arrives with an owner and a runbook, and runs as a ticket for two weeks
choices.why: A new paging alert comes with its runbook and owner in the same change and starts as a ticket. Two weeks show how often it would have paged, and whether anybody would have acted.

choices.text: It pages, and the team reviews it after its first false alarm at night
choices.why: Waiting for the first false page is paying for the lesson in somebody's sleep, and every false page spends the credibility of the true ones.

prompt: HR asks the tech lead for each developer's items finished last quarter, for the performance reviews. Which of these contributions would that count leave out? Choose every one that applies.
hint: Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 8; Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 10.

choices.text: Reviewing colleagues' changes before starting anything new
choices.why: Review first is why the cycle time fell, and every week spent reviewing lowered the reviewer's own count.

choices.text: Persuading another team to make the change a blocked item needed
choices.why: Whoever unblocks the stuck item does the week's most valuable work and closes no item of their own.

choices.text: Pairing with a colleague on the oldest item on the board
choices.why: Two people on one item finish it sooner and count once, so one of them is invisible.

choices.text: Restoring card charges at two in the morning
choices.why: The person who restored service has an empty history for the next day, and nothing on the board records the night.

choices.text: Finishing a large feature alone over three weeks
choices.why: A finished item is exactly what the count sees. What it measures badly is size, not whether the item is there.

choices.text: Closing a long run of small bug tickets
choices.why: The count sees these, and rewards them: items finished per person measures who takes small items.

prompt: Under the Billing team's SLI for card charges, which of these charge attempts count as good events? Choose every one that applies.
hint: Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 16.

choices.text: A card with no funds, declined in two seconds for the bank's reason
choices.why: A decline the bank gave, answered quickly, is the service working. Counting it as bad would make the SLI fall whenever shoppers run out of money.

choices.text: A charge approved once, for the right amount, in four seconds
choices.why: Answered within ten seconds, charged exactly once and correctly: that is the definition of a good event.

choices.text: A charge approved once, for the right amount, after twenty-five seconds
choices.why: Slow is bad. A shop owner with a queue cannot tell a forty-second payment from a failed one, so the threshold is ten seconds.

choices.text: A charge the provider approved, and the card was charged twice
choices.why: Charging twice is the worst answer there is. An SLI that only asked whether the provider said yes would have scored 30 September a success.

choices.text: A charge that timed out and got no answer at all
choices.why: No answer is an availability failure, the first of the three things folded into this SLI.

choices.text: A charge approved once in one second, for the wrong amount
choices.why: Correctness is part of the SLI: charged once, the right amount. A fast wrong answer is still a wrong answer.

prompt: Under the lesson's working definition of an incident, which of these should be declared as one? Choose every one that applies.
hint: Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 13.

choices.text: Card payments for one card brand have been failing since noon
choices.why: Unplanned, harming users, needing several people now: in the Billing team's scale it is a SEV2.

choices.text: The monthly statement job failed at 05:00 on the 1st, for every shop
choices.why: The statement is due by 06:00 on the 1st, and every shop will miss it. Harm to users that cannot wait for the next planning meeting is an incident, whatever caused it.

choices.text: A shop reports that it was charged twice for its subscription
choices.why: One double charge on a payments product is enough to ask. Declaring costs one command, and a false alarm closed in ten minutes is a success.

choices.text: The team's internal dashboard of review times has stopped loading
choices.why: Nobody who uses the service is harmed. A broken internal dashboard is a bug, handled as normal work.

choices.text: A planned database maintenance window is running exactly to plan
choices.why: A maintenance window that goes as planned is not unplanned, so it fails the first part of the definition.

choices.text: A typo has appeared in the footer of the printed invoices
choices.why: Cosmetic, the bottom of the scale: a normal ticket, not an incident.

prompt: A tech lead is choosing a whole-board work-in-progress limit for a Kanban board. Over two stable months the team finished 0.8 items a day, counting calendar days, and it wants items to take 10 days on average from start to finish. By Little's law, how many items should be open on an average day? Answer in items.
hint: Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 1; Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 3.

prompt: A team finishes 1.5 items a day and takes its backlog oldest first. 36 accepted requests are waiting ahead of a new one. Applying Little's law to the backlog, as the lesson does, how many days will the new request wait before anybody starts it? Answer in days.
hint: Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 2.

prompt: A checkout service has an objective of 99.95% of requests good over a rolling 30 days. Turned into continuous downtime, the way the lesson's table of nines does it, how many minutes of total failure does the error budget allow in 30 days? Answer in minutes.
hint: Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 16.

prompt: A team wrote down, before looking, that a change failure is a deployment that causes an incident of SEV2 or worse. Last quarter it made 80 deployments. Three of them caused SEV1 or SEV2 incidents, two caused SEV3 incidents, and a separate SEV1 came from a card provider's outage with no deployment involved. What was the change failure rate, in percent?
hint: Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 5.

prompt: Planning a quarter the way the lesson does, the 85% answer from the throughput forecast is 80 items. The tech lead commits 75% of that number to planned work and leaves the rest for what arrives. How many planned items does the quarter commit to? Answer in items.
hint: Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 12.

prompt: The head of product says: "Four days is great. Let's commit to three next quarter." The rule Bia answers with: report the measure; target the ___.
hint: Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 20; Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 13.

prompt: At 18:02 Rafa is fairly sure which of the four changes is at fault and wants half an hour to confirm it. The order the lesson gives for an incident: mitigate, then ___, then fix.
hint: Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 14.

prompt: Put the parts of Bia's one-page quarterly review in the order the page gives them.
hint: Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 19.
items: The headline: three sentences, the good news and the bad together
What changed, and why, one line of cause per finding
What went wrong
What happens next
What we need: asks somebody in the room can say yes or no to
trap: Putting what happens next, or what we need, before what went wrong is the usual slip: a feature freeze is unreasonable on its own and obvious after the incident and the budget.

prompt: Put the steps for planning a quarter without filling it in the order the lesson gives.
hint: Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 12.
items: Start from the team's measured throughput
Run the forecast for the quarter's days and take the 85% answer
Commit 70 to 80% of that number to planned work
Put everything else below a line, in order
Re-forecast every week and move the line
trap: The usual order starts from headcount times weeks and fills the result; committing before forecasting, or planning to the full 85% number, leaves nothing to absorb the unplanned work the history says will come.

prompt: Match each situation in an incident to the mitigation the lesson's table fits to it.
hint: Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 14.

pairs.left: The harm began with this afternoon's release
The change causing the harm was released behind a flag
One region is failing and the other is healthy
pairs.right: fail over to the other region

pairs.left: A traffic spike is overwhelming the service

right_distractors: find the bug and fix it first

prompt: Using the Billing team's severity scale, match each first report to the level it is declared at.
hint: Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 13.

pairs.left: A release makes every shop's invoice show the wrong tax amount
Payments with one card brand fail, and shops can still pay by bank transfer
Filtering last year's statements by date takes a minute instead of a second
The internal admin page shows last year's logo

right_distractors: not graded until the cause is known

prompt: A tech lead's status note says the database migration "will take 13.5 days". Her honest estimate is somewhere between two and four weeks. What is wrong with the note?
hint: Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 1.

choices.text: False precision, read as a confidence she does not have
choices.why: Right. A number sharper than the estimate is planned around as if it were a measurement; the range is the honest statement.

choices.text: Nothing: one exact number is easier for the reader to plan around than a range
choices.why: The reader does plan around it, and that is the problem: the plan rests on a certainty nobody had.

choices.text: It should say "soon" instead, since nobody can be sure of the date yet
choices.why: "Soon" hides the uncertainty instead of stating it; the reader guesses a number and it is rarely hers.

choices.text: It should round the figure to 14 days so that it reads less fussy
choices.why: Rounding keeps a single number pretending to certainty; the two-to-four-week range is what she actually knows.

prompt: A tech lead drafts her team's one-page technical strategy, starting from the one-pager she uses for proposals. Which part does the strategy page need that a proposal page does not?
hint: Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 2; Technical Strategy: Debt, Budget and Build versus Buy, lesson 3.

choices.text: A block saying what happens if we do nothing
choices.why: That block belongs to the proposal one-pager, where it turns a request into a decision; it is not what the strategy page adds.

choices.text: A header naming its owner, who signed it and the next review date
choices.why: Right. The page is quoted in arguments for months, by people deciding things it never mentions, and a quotation needs a source with a date.

choices.text: The incident analysis in full, so that anybody can check the diagnosis
choices.why: The strategy page links the evidence and leaves it out; its reader needs the conclusion, and the reviewer knows where to look.

choices.text: One named decider and a date by which the decision is due
choices.why: That is the proposal's ask: one person, one decision. A strategy is a tool for hundreds of later decisions.

prompt: A year after the connections RFC was accepted, the team replaces fixed quotas with a different approach. A colleague offers to edit the RFC and its decision record so that both describe the new design and the documentation is current. What should happen instead?
hint: Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 2; Technical Strategy: Debt, Budget and Build versus Buy, lesson 17.

choices.text: Edit the decision record, which is documentation, and leave the RFC as history
choices.why: An accepted record is never edited: rewriting it erases the reasoning that was right at the time, and the log stops explaining how the system got here.

choices.text: Delete both, since a record about a design that is gone misleads the next engineer
choices.why: The old record answers "why did we ever do that?", the same job a rejected RFC does; deleting it invites somebody to repeat the argument.

choices.text: Leave both as written, record the new decision apart, mark the old one superseded
choices.why: Right. The old record changes in one line, its status, and the two point at each other; the RFC keeps its final status where people can find it.

choices.text: Reopen the old RFC for comment and rewrite it once the new design is accepted
choices.why: An RFC is written before a decision and argues for one option; the new decision gets its own process and record, and the old RFC stays as decided.

prompt: Put the six blocks of a one-pager in order, from the top of the page down.
hint: Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 2.
items: A title that is the decision
The ask: who decides, what, and by when
The problem, with its size
The proposal, in the decider's words
Cost and risk
What happens if we do nothing
trap: Opening with the problem puts the investigation's order back on the page. The ask comes second so the decider knows what is wanted before the reasons, and "if we do nothing" closes it because that block turns the ask into a choice.

prompt: An architect needs three engineer-weeks from the mobile team in June and writes to the head of product. Which sentence does her message most need?
hint: Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 3.

choices.text: The work cuts p95 latency on the order page from 2.4 s to 800 ms
choices.why: That is the team's unit. Product decides in scope, dates and customer impact, and latency means nothing until it becomes one of those.

choices.text: The change is small and low-risk, so it should not need a long discussion
choices.why: Adjectives with no trade-off in them; the request is still three weeks taken from something she promised somebody.

choices.text: The board has already heard about it and expects it done by June
choices.why: Invoking another audience is pressure, not the trade-off she actually decides on.

choices.text: The loyalty screen moves from June to the first week of July
choices.why: Right. Product owns the order things are built in, so the message names what it displaces, or she works it out herself, usually less kindly.

prompt: A tech lead has ten minutes with the CFO to get a fix approved. His plan is to take the architecture deck he showed the engineers and strip out the jargon so that a non-engineer can follow it. What is wrong with the plan?
hint: Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 3; Technical Strategy: Debt, Budget and Build versus Buy, lesson 20.

choices.text: It simplifies the mechanism, when the CFO needs a slide about consequences
choices.why: Right. Adapting a message changes its unit, not its difficulty; an executive slide is about consequences, and a simplified mechanism is too technical for the CFO and too vague for the CTO.

choices.text: Nothing, provided every remaining term is defined the first time it appears
choices.why: Defining terms cures jargon, but the deck still answers how the system works, which nobody in the room asked.

choices.text: Nothing, provided a good analogy carries the hardest slide of the deck
choices.why: An analogy helps one point and breaks somewhere; it does not turn a deck about mechanism into one about consequences.

choices.text: It needs cutting down to the three slides that matter most to the CFO
choices.why: Three slides of the same kind are still a tour of the work; the CFO needs the four questions answered, starting with the decision.

prompt: Marola moves product search to a hosted service. Match each sentence to the reader whose version of the announcement it belongs in.
hint: Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 3.

pairs.left: Cuts R$ 12,000 a month and removes the risk of search failing on campaign days
Takes three engineer-weeks, so the loyalty screen moves from May to June
New prices reach search up to a minute late, so do not use it to confirm a write
From Tuesday the 9th your shoppers see results in a new order; nothing is needed from you

prompt: A tech lead prices a weekly checkout failure. Every Saturday 5,000 checkouts are attempted and 3% fail; 40% of the customers who fail do not come back to order; the average basket is R$ 200 and gross margin is 25%. Over 52 Saturdays, how much margin is lost in a year, in reais?
hint: Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 4.

prompt: Two lock-ins are on a tech lead's list. Leaving the managed queue would cost R$ 300,000, with a 5% chance of switching in three years. Leaving the email provider would cost R$ 100,000, with a 40% chance. Building portability for either one costs R$ 20,000. What does pricing them as risks decide?
hint: Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 4; Technical Strategy: Debt, Budget and Build versus Buy, lesson 10.

choices.text: Pay for the queue first, since leaving it would cost three times as much
choices.why: Switching cost alone ignores the likelihood. The queue's expected cost is 5% of R$ 300,000, R$ 15,000, less than the R$ 20,000 that avoiding it costs.

choices.text: Accept the queue lock-in and pay to make the email provider portable
choices.why: Right. Expected cost is likelihood times impact: R$ 15,000 for the queue, below the price of portability, and R$ 40,000 for the email provider, twice it.

choices.text: Pay for both, since avoiding lock-in is the prudent default
choices.why: That is the slogan, and it cannot say when to stop paying; for the queue the protection costs more than the risk it removes.

choices.text: Pay for neither, since both probabilities are just judgements
choices.why: A judgement stated with its reasons is still the number to compare, and the email provider is far from its break-even: the decision holds down to a 20% chance.

prompt: The finance director decides, knowingly, to carry a database risk until the April work. Which of these does the entry in the risk register need? Choose all that apply.
hint: Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 4.

choices.text: The name of the person who accepted it
choices.why: Yes. An acceptance with a name on it is a decision; one without a name is a default nobody took.

choices.text: The date it will be looked at again
choices.why: Yes. A review date stops an acceptance from quietly becoming permanent.

choices.text: What would trigger an earlier review
choices.why: Yes. At Marola the trigger fired on 6 March, and nobody had to argue about reopening the decision.

choices.text: The engineer who first raised it
choices.why: The entry records the decision and when it is reopened, not who noticed the risk.

choices.text: One expected-loss figure, without a range
choices.why: Not one of the three things the entry carries, and lesson 4 prefers a range with what it rests on.

choices.text: The vendor's uptime guarantee
choices.why: That belongs to transferring a risk, a different response; an accepted risk needs who, when, and the trigger.

prompt: Near the end of a decision presentation, the head of sales says: "This is a lot of money for a problem we only have on Saturdays." What is the better next move?
hint: Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 5.

choices.text: Show the loss table again, more slowly, so the size of the problem lands
choices.why: Re-arguing the merits answers the surface of the objection; the concern underneath may have nothing to do with the numbers.

choices.text: Ask the CEO in the room to rule on it, since it is above the presenter
choices.why: Calling for a ruling in the meeting turns a question into a contest the objector now has to lose in public.

choices.text: Find the concern under it: the cost, the risk of the change, or something of hers it touches
choices.why: Right. An objection is information; at Marola, Renata's objection to the timing turned out to be a promise she had made to the stores, settled once Lívia asked about it.

choices.text: Offer to cut the scope until the cost falls under her threshold
choices.why: Conceding before knowing the concern can give away the fix and still leave her worry untouched.

prompt: A strategy review gets a single slide. Which title passes both the assertion-evidence rule and the stricter test that the decision survives if only the title does?
hint: Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 5; Technical Strategy: Debt, Budget and Build versus Buy, lesson 20.

choices.text: Reservation module: the current state, four options and our proposal
choices.why: A topic. It tells the room what the slide is about and gives them nothing to agree or disagree with.

choices.text: Row locks in the reservation module queue up and time out under on-sale load
choices.why: A full-sentence claim, so it passes lesson 5, but it asks for nothing: true sentences can still leave no decision behind.

choices.text: Every option except doing nothing costs less than one year of failed on-sales
choices.why: A good assertion for an options slide; read alone, though, nobody could say yes or no to it.

choices.text: Approve the seat-hold fix by March: R$ 48,000 once against R$ 364,800 a year
choices.why: Right. If the slide were lost and the title survived, the CFO could still say yes or no: what, by when, and the two numbers.

prompt: Christensen's idea, applied to a request: customers do not want a product as such; they hire it to get a ___ done, and understanding that tells you what to build.
hint: Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 6.

prompt: A tech lead asks the head of sales "Why do you want a dashboard?" and gets a defensive reply. Which question asks for the same information and is heard as curiosity?
hint: Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 6.

choices.text: "What would be different for your team if it existed?"
choices.why: Right. It asks for the effect, which is where the need lives, without asking her to justify herself.

choices.text: "Is the dashboard the priority for this quarter?"
choices.why: A closed question: it can be answered with a word and only confirms or denies a guess.

choices.text: "Have you checked whether the weekly report covers it?"
choices.why: Closed, and it imports the asker's guess into the answer.

choices.text: "Could you justify the dashboard in one sentence?"
choices.why: It is the same challenge as "why", made more explicit.

prompt: A team asked an internal consultant to help them pick a message broker. Her count shows that none of their seven incidents came from the problem a broker solves. How does her written diagnosis treat the broker?
hint: Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 7.

choices.text: It leaves the broker out, because the data has already ruled it out
choices.why: Dropping the client's idea makes the diagnosis feel imposed, and the broker can still help for a different reason.

choices.text: As one option, for the reason it would really help
choices.why: Right. At Marola it was option 3, separate data kept in step by events; saying where the idea fits lets them accept a diagnosis that started elsewhere.

choices.text: It recommends the broker anyway, to keep the team's goodwill
choices.why: A recommendation the data contradicts spends the consultant's credibility; the goodwill comes from treating the idea fairly.

choices.text: It names who proposed the broker, so the choice has an owner
choices.why: The note attaches no names to anything; the owner of the choice is the team, as the contract said.

prompt: A strategy fences off the reservation path until a load test passes. Product asks for group holds, and the tech lead's no offers "a simpler version of group holds" as the alternative. What is wrong with it?
hint: Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 8; Technical Strategy: Debt, Budget and Build versus Buy, lesson 19.

choices.text: Nothing: "not all of it" is the alternative the lesson says is most often missed
choices.why: A smaller version is a good alternative in general; with a strategy, it also has to stay inside the guiding policy.

choices.text: He should offer no alternative, because the strategy already gives the reason
choices.why: A no without an alternative ends the conversation; the strategy shapes the alternative, it does not remove it.

choices.text: It still changes the fenced path, so it is the same request made smaller
choices.why: Right. It meets the same objection with less to offer; an alternative has to serve the need and stay inside the policy, like the Box Office group code.

choices.text: It should carry a date for the full version instead of offering a smaller one
choices.why: The date is a different part, when the answer changes; it does not replace an alternative that serves the need now.

prompt: A tech lead answers a request with "we'll look at it later". Product tells the client something is coming, and at the next planning it turns out nothing was ever scheduled. What should the answer have been?
hint: Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 8; Technical Strategy: Debt, Budget and Build versus Buy, lesson 19.

choices.text: A yes with best efforts, since the client relationship outweighs the schedule
choices.why: A vague yes is the worst answer: the asker plans around it, the team cannot deliver it, and the disappointment lands on the day it matters.

choices.text: A plain no with the reason, because any condition softens the refusal
choices.why: A condition does the reverse, committing the team to a yes on the day it holds; a bare no fits only when nothing observable would change it.

choices.text: The same "later", with the reasons for the delay written in the ticket
choices.why: Reasons with no condition and no review date still give the asker nothing to watch, and it decays the same way.

choices.text: Not yet, with a checkable condition and a day a named person looks again
choices.why: Right. The condition says what would change the answer, and the review date stops "not yet" from decaying into the "later" that was delivered months late.

prompt: Two teams cannot agree whether a shared migration or a client feature goes first in March, and neither lead has the authority to trade one team's priorities against the other's. What do both courses recommend?
hint: Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 9; Leading People: One-to-Ones, Feedback and Hiring, lesson 22.

choices.text: One page written together: the facts both accept, each side's view, the decision needed
choices.why: Right. The person deciding hears one account of the facts rather than two, and decides on them instead of on whose manager spoke first.

choices.text: Each lead briefs their own director first, so both framings get heard
choices.why: A dispute escalated by each side separately arrives as two accusations, heard at different times, each defensively.

choices.text: The mediator decides, since both leads have said they would accept it
choices.why: A mediator who decides becomes the owner of every future argument about it, and a business priority is above both of them anyway.

choices.text: Settle it in the shared channel, where everybody affected sees the reasoning
choices.why: In public everybody performs for the audience, and nobody can change position without losing face.

prompt: A junior cannot yet run a design review alone, but can with one or two questions at the right moment. Vygotsky called that space the zone of ___ development.
hint: Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 10.

prompt: A mentor decides how much of each decision on a stretch assignment to hand to the junior. Put these from least handed over to most.
hint: Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 10.
items: "Do this, this way."
"Look into it and tell me what you'd do; I'll decide."
"Decide, and tell me before you act."
"Decide and act; tell me afterwards."
"Decide and act; you don't need to tell me."
trap: The usual slip is swapping the middle rungs. "Tell me before you act" still lets the mentor stop a mistake and "tell me afterwards" does not, which is why the risky part of a change stays lower on the ladder than the rest.

prompt: A senior reviewer wants a junior's pull request to teach the team what good looks like here. Which comments do that? Choose all that apply.
hint: Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 11; Leading People: One-to-Ones, Feedback and Hiring, lesson 9.

choices.text: praise: splitting the rename from the fix let each be read on its own
choices.why: Yes. It names a choice and why it mattered, so the author repeats it on purpose and everybody reading the review learns the bar.

choices.text: praise: each test name says what it checks, so a failure explains itself
choices.why: Yes. Specific praise is calibration: it says which choices were deliberate good ones.

choices.text: LGTM, great work on this one, really happy with how it turned out!
choices.why: Pleasant and empty: great in what way, compared with what, for whom?

choices.text: You're a natural at this kind of code, honestly one of our best.
choices.why: Praise for a trait teaches people to protect the label; praise for a choice teaches them to repeat it.

choices.text: Nice overall, but the naming needs another pass; still really solid work.
choices.why: The sandwich: after a few of these, every compliment is heard as the warning before a "but".

choices.text: Thanks, team, for another clean change that went through without a fuss.
choices.why: It credits nobody precisely and names no choice, so nobody learns what to do again.

prompt: Strong-style pairing has one rule: for an idea to go from your head into the computer, it must go through someone else's ___.
hint: Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 12.

prompt: Before a deadline negotiation, a tech lead has two numbers for the order state machine: 25 engineer-days a year spent on workarounds, and R$ 90,000 a year of revenue lost to its incidents. He plans to add them into one total for the director. What is the better presentation?
hint: Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 13; Technical Strategy: Debt, Budget and Build versus Buy, lesson 20.

choices.text: One total, because a single large number is what wins against a feature
choices.why: Adding salary time to lost revenue mixes two kinds of money, and the first person in finance to notice discounts the whole total.

choices.text: Two lines: salary time already paid, and revenue that never arrives
choices.why: Right. Each is interest stated in the director's unit and each can be set against the three-week fix on its own, which is stronger than a sum.

choices.text: The revenue alone, since engineers' time is already paid for and costs nothing
choices.why: Workaround time is real interest, a month a year not spent on something else; it is a different kind of money, not free.

choices.text: Neither figure; say the code is a mess that slows down every change
choices.why: An adjective cannot be weighed against a feature; the numbers are what make the debt a trade.

prompt: Product wants a feature live on 1 December and the team's estimate does not fit. A director suggests the team be "a bit less thorough with testing" to make it. Who owns that call, and what follows?
hint: Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 13.

choices.text: Product, because product owns the promise to customers and the date
choices.why: Product owns scope and the date; quality belongs to the team that will live with the result.

choices.text: The director, because he sees every team's dates at once
choices.why: Seniority is not ownership of the lever, and the director will not be the one carrying the consequences in January.

choices.text: The tech lead: a shortcut is said aloud, priced and written down as debt, or not taken
choices.why: Right. Quality is the lever nobody sees move; if nobody would agree to the shortcut out loud, the team does not take it quietly.

choices.text: Nobody needs to, since testing effort is invisible to customers at launch
choices.why: That invisibility is exactly why quality looks like a lever; the cost arrives later and nobody connects it to the decision.

prompt: Twenty minutes into a checkout outage, match each audience to what its message has to give it.
hint: Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 14.

pairs.left: support
pairs.right: a true sentence to say to the next customer

pairs.left: leadership
pairs.right: the impact in business terms, and whether to act

pairs.left: customers
pairs.right: whether it affects them, and when to try again

pairs.left: a client chain
pairs.right: a direct message from its account owner

right_distractors: every log line, as it happens
the suspected cause, as soon as there is one

prompt: Which of these postmortem timeline entries are written the way a blameless review asks? Choose all that apply.
hint: Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 15.

choices.text: 19:05 Paulo starts the zone backfill; the runbook says nothing of peak hours
choices.why: Yes. It says what he did and what he could see, and leaves the evaluation to the analysis of the system.

choices.text: 19:05 Paulo carelessly runs the backfill in the middle of the busy evening peak
choices.why: "Carelessly" is a verdict, and "in the middle of peak" judges him for something nobody had told him mattered.

choices.text: 19:16 a checkout-error alert pages Bruna; it names checkout, not the database
choices.why: Yes. It records what the commander could see, which explains the next twelve minutes better than any judgement.

choices.text: 19:19 Bruna wastes twelve minutes chasing a deploy nobody had made
choices.why: Hindsight: at that minute a bad deploy was the usual cause and a reasonable guess.

choices.text: 19:31 Lucas sees connections at the limit and asks who ran the job
choices.why: Yes. A fact, and the decision it led to.

choices.text: 19:36 Paulo finally replies in the channel, after having gone home early
choices.why: "Finally" and "early" carry blame; he stopped the job as soon as he was asked.

prompt: An engineer's staff case failed for "no influence beyond the team". Two other teams have asked him privately about his retry design. He asks whether he should start a public blog and apply to conferences. What do the two courses point to first?
hint: Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 16; Leading People: One-to-Ones, Feedback and Hiring, lesson 13.

choices.text: Start the blog now, since an outside audience is the quickest way to get noticed
choices.why: A reputation outside the company that is not matched inside it is fragile; the rings go team, company, community.

choices.text: Move him onto a more visible project, because his current work is hidden
choices.why: The work is not invisible, it is undescribed; growing in visibility is the same work made legible.

choices.text: Post regularly about his achievements to build a personal brand
choices.why: Engineers find out within a conversation when the record behind the posts is thin.

choices.text: Write it up for all of engineering and present it at the architecture review
choices.why: Right. It is the work two teams already asked about, made visible inside the company, which is both the evidence the case lacked and the next ring of a reputation.

prompt: A food-delivery company's strategy page lists, under its actions: "All teams are encouraged to consider reliability in their planning, on an ongoing basis." By the lesson's test for an action, what is wrong with this line?
hint: Technical Strategy: Debt, Budget and Build versus Buy, lesson 1.

choices.text: It names no owner, no start date and nothing it replaces
choices.why: The test for an action is who does it, from when, instead of what. "All teams" and "ongoing" are the failing answers the lesson lists, so the line commits nobody.

choices.text: It is a superlative with no mechanism, which makes it fluff
choices.why: Fluff is a line like "the most reliable platform in Brazil". This one claims nothing grand; its fault is that it commits nobody to anything.

choices.text: It sets a target and says nothing about how to reach it
choices.why: That is mistaking a goal for strategy, as with "reach 99.99%". This line has no target in it at all.

choices.text: It covers reliability alone, while the company has other problems
choices.why: Choosing one problem is what a strategy is for. Narrowness is not the fault; committing nothing is.

prompt: A retailer's strategy has the action "every service has a named owner by the end of Q2". The roadmap shows it in Q2, but no team's backlog has an item for it, and two teams each assume the other will do it. In the lesson's terms, what is this action?
hint: Technical Strategy: Debt, Budget and Build versus Buy, lesson 2.

choices.text: An orphan: work with no reason above it in the strategy
choices.why: An orphan runs the other way: work in a backlog that traces up to nothing. Here the reason exists and the work does not.

choices.text: Keeping the lights on, to be labelled honestly as such
choices.why: That label is for work forced from outside, such as a framework past its supported life. This is an action the strategy chose.

choices.text: Decoration: a promise with no work below it
choices.why: Traced down, the action stops at the roadmap. The trace makes that impersonal: either a backlog item exists or it does not.

choices.text: A roadmap doing the job that a strategy should be doing
choices.why: The strategy exists and named the action. The failure sits below the roadmap, not in place of the strategy.

prompt: Coreto's on-sale load test takes a month longer than planned. The sales director asks Davi for "the date" the deploy freeze will be automated, to plan the festival season around it. By both lessons, what should Davi do?
hint: Technical Strategy: Debt, Budget and Build versus Buy, lesson 2; Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 11.

choices.text: Rewrite the strategy around the new date, since one of its actions moved
choices.why: A strategy rewritten each time a date slips was the roadmap again. The diagnosis has not changed, so the strategy stays.

choices.text: Give one firm date with a quiet buffer, so it cannot be missed
choices.why: A secret buffer is found out the first time the team finishes early, and every later forecast is discounted.

choices.text: Keep the old quarter on the roadmap, since sales plans against it
choices.why: Absorbing change cheaply is the roadmap's job. A quarter known to be wrong has sales planning against a fiction.

choices.text: Move the roadmap line, keep the strategy, and give a range with odds
choices.why: The roadmap moves and the strategy does not. A date stated as a probability, with when it will be updated, is one sales can plan on.

prompt: Two weeks after a strategy page goes out, a tech lead asks five people to say it back. One engineer answers: "We're moving off the monolith, slowly." The page's not list says the migration is off for the year. What does the lesson read in that answer?
hint: Technical Strategy: Debt, Budget and Build versus Buy, lesson 3.

choices.text: Close enough: the engineer kept the spirit of the page, which is what the test checks
choices.why: The answer says the opposite of the page. A slow migration is still the migration the not list rules out.

choices.text: A version of the strategy nobody wrote is going round, deciding things
choices.why: The lesson calls it the most useful answer in the table: it shows which version is making decisions now.

choices.text: The engineer did not read the page, which is for his manager to raise rather than the author
choices.why: The lesson reads failures as pointing at the page and how it was delivered, not at the five people.

choices.text: The not list was too blunt, and softening it would stop people resisting the page
choices.why: A not list nobody complains about was written to avoid complaint. The fix was moving the policy and the list, and reading it aloud.

prompt: An online shop's tax code is slow and risky to change, because every state has its own rules and the law changes twice a year. Nobody can describe a design that would make it simpler. By the lesson's two questions, what is it?
hint: Technical Strategy: Debt, Budget and Build versus Buy, lesson 4.

choices.text: Debt with interest, to be put in the register and priced
choices.why: It fails the first question: nobody can name a better design, so there is nothing to repay.

choices.text: Debt that charges nothing, and can be left where it is
choices.why: That box is a better design with no cost. This code costs something on every change.

choices.text: The problem itself: it needs tests and documentation
choices.why: There is a cost and no better design: the difficulty belongs to the domain, and a refactoring would be a search for something that does not exist.

choices.text: A reckless, inadvertent debt left by people who missed layering
choices.why: The quadrant sorts how a debt came to exist. This is not a debt, so there is nothing to sort.

prompt: A rewrite proposal says it pays for itself three years after it ships, and building it takes two years. Through the build the old system's interest is still paid in full. By the lesson's arithmetic, about when is the money back, counted from the first commit?
hint: Technical Strategy: Debt, Budget and Build versus Buy, lesson 6.

choices.text: After about five years: the build, then the payback
choices.why: The payback clock starts when the new system ships, so the two periods add. Coreto's proposal came back about seven years in for the same reason.

choices.text: After about three years, as the proposal itself says
choices.why: The proposal's three years are counted from the switch, not from the first commit.

choices.text: After about two years, on the day the new system ships
choices.why: Shipping starts the saving; it does not return the cost already spent.

choices.text: After about one year, since the old interest stops once work begins
choices.why: During the build the old system keeps running and its interest is paid in full. Nothing is saved until the switch.

prompt: A year later, Coreto's new strategy decides to win venues on discovery: recommending the next show to each buyer, filling seats the venue could not fill alone. The Catalogue lead says the search decision is settled, because search was classified as context. What does the lesson say?
hint: Technical Strategy: Debt, Budget and Build versus Buy, lesson 8.

choices.text: It stays settled: search is critical context and must not break down
choices.why: Critical context is still context, but the classification itself has moved with the strategy.

choices.text: Reopen it: core moves with the strategy, and search with it too
choices.why: Core moves when the strategy changes. Winning on discovery makes ranking something venues could choose Coreto for, so building is a serious option again.

choices.text: Leave it until the vendor's yearly rise passes the agreed cap
choices.why: A price rise is a question for the exit and the lock-in. What changed here is what Coreto competes on.

choices.text: Reopen it, because whatever a team wants to build is core to that team
choices.why: That is the trap the lesson names, not a reason. The question to ask is whether a venue would notice and leave.

prompt: Rafaela asks Otávio to move two Platform engineers onto the on-sale load test for a quarter. Her request reads: "Line: People. No new money: both are already on the payroll." Otávio sends it back. Of the lesson's questions it leaves unanswered, which is the one the lesson says a CFO checks first?
hint: Technical Strategy: Debt, Budget and Build versus Buy, lesson 11.

choices.text: Which line: a load test belongs under tooling, not people
choices.why: Two people changing what they work on is the people line, and she named it correctly.

choices.text: How much: two engineers for a quarter is R$ 132,000 of new money
choices.why: It is R$ 132,000 of time, but not new money; the company pays it either way. What it buys elsewhere is the question.

choices.text: When: a request made outside the budget round is read last
choices.why: Timing is a handicap the lesson names, but the gap a CFO checks first is in the request itself.

choices.text: What waits: the work those two stop doing
choices.why: Most requests move people already paid, and the cost is paid in whatever they stop doing. It is the question requests leave out most often.

prompt: At the quarterly review, the engineering director sees that 18 of 26 new services started from Platform's template and proposes 90% as next quarter's target. What should Rafaela answer, by both lessons?
hint: Technical Strategy: Debt, Budget and Build versus Buy, lesson 14; Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 19.

choices.text: Agree, and add a review that checks every new service uses it
choices.why: A checked requirement measures obedience. The teams with a sound reason to leave would stay on and work around it, and the reason would never arrive.

choices.text: Report the share and why some went elsewhere; set no target
choices.why: A target turns a measurement into a goal that gets met by relabelling. Report the measure; target the practice.

choices.text: Raise it to 100%, since a path that teams skip has failed
choices.why: A share that stays off by choice is healthy: Data's nightly jobs belong off the path.

choices.text: Agree to 90%, counting only services that still take its updates
choices.why: Staying on the path is the better thing to count, but a target on it invites the same games.

prompt: After an incident, Checkout's on-call engineers open a pull request that raises checkout's objective from 99.9% to 99.99% in the alerting configuration. By both lessons, what should the tech lead do with it?
hint: Technical Strategy: Debt, Budget and Build versus Buy, lesson 16; Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 16.

choices.text: Merge it: an alerting threshold is an engineering setting
choices.why: That is the disguise. The number is a promise to venues and a claim on engineering's time, and it reached the queue in technical words.

choices.text: Set checkout to 100%, since every failed checkout loses a sale
choices.why: 100% forbids change and cannot be met, so it stops meaning anything from the second month.

choices.text: Merge it, and let the error budget settle any argument later
choices.why: A budget settles the argument because both sides signed the objective. One chosen by on-call alone has skipped that.

choices.text: Take it to product and the CTO as options: four minutes a month, slower releases
choices.why: The objective is a product decision. 99.99% allows about four minutes of bad charges a month and makes every release more expensive; product signs it beside the team.

prompt: Over one quarter, Checkout receives four requests of about 90 hours each, and Mateus agrees to each one because "it is only a quarter of a sprint". By both lessons, what has happened?
hint: Technical Strategy: Debt, Budget and Build versus Buy, lesson 19; Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 12.

choices.text: Nothing serious: each was small, and each was judged on its merits
choices.why: Each was judged against nothing. Compared with the sprint, four of them are the whole of it.

choices.text: The team spent its slack, which is what slack is there for
choices.why: Slack is room left on purpose. Checkout's 360 hours were all promised to the move onto the hold interface, so none of them were slack.

choices.text: A sprint of the strategy's work has gone, and no one decision moved it
choices.why: Four times 90 is 360, a whole Checkout sprint. A team planned to its full capacity takes work on only by dropping something nobody chose to drop.

choices.text: The hours should have been folded into the estimates of the strategy's work
choices.why: Hiding work in estimates teaches product to discount every estimate, the honest ones included.

prompt: After Davi's slide, a board member says: "So we will lose about one on-sale this year, R$ 364,800." By both lessons, what should Davi answer?
hint: Technical Strategy: Debt, Budget and Build versus Buy, lesson 20; Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 11.

choices.text: No: an average over many years; some have none, some two
choices.why: Expected value is right for comparing with a price paid once and for sizing a reserve across many risks, and wrong as a forecast of one year. Two failures would cost R$ 760,000.

choices.text: Yes: 0.96 failures a year rounds to one, so that is the forecast
choices.why: A count of failures is a whole number, and the expected one is an average. Presented as a forecast it looks wrong in the first quiet year.

choices.text: No: that is the worst case, if every big on-sale failed
choices.why: If all twelve failed the year would cost R$ 4,560,000. R$ 364,800 is weighted by the 8%.

choices.text: No: it is the price of the fix spread over twelve on-sales
choices.why: The fix is R$ 48,000, paid once. The R$ 364,800 is the expected loss it is set against.

prompt: A product manager scores Coreto's four items in WSJF points, as the management course teaches, and gets the same order as the CD3 sheet. She says the reais add nothing. What does the lesson on cost of delay say money adds that points do not?
hint: Technical Strategy: Debt, Budget and Build versus Buy, lesson 13; Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 12.

choices.text: Precision: reais make each estimate exact to the real
choices.why: The lesson says the estimates are honest about being estimates; the method needs no more precision than points.

choices.text: A way to rank fixed-date items, which points cannot place
choices.why: Lesson 13 does not rank a fixed-date item with CD3 either: it is scheduled to land before its date, and the rest is ordered around it.

choices.text: A confidence term, so a hunch weighs less than a measurement
choices.why: Neither formula has one; confidence is what RICE adds and WSJF lacks.

choices.text: A size for the gap between two orders, set beside the price of a hire
choices.why: Points give a ranking and say nothing about what ignoring it loses. R$ 162,000 is more than half an engineer-year, and it sits beside anything else the company spends.

prompt: Festival organisers sign their contracts for the season on 1 September: nothing is lost before that day, and the season is lost after it. Júlia enters festival seat maps in the CD3 sheet at a steady R$ 30,000 a week. By both lessons, what is wrong?
hint: Technical Strategy: Debt, Budget and Build versus Buy, lesson 13; Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 12.

choices.text: Nothing: a steady rate is the standard profile for features
choices.why: Standard fits most features, and this one has a fixed date. Put through a steady-rate formula, it comes out in the wrong place.

choices.text: The weekly figure is too low to put the item first
choices.why: The size of the estimate is not the fault; its shape is. Raising it to win would be forcing an input.

choices.text: It is a fixed-date item: schedule it before 1 September, order the rest
choices.why: A fixed-date item is not ranked by CD3. It is scheduled late enough to fit other work and early enough to be sure, and the queue is ordered around it.

choices.text: It belongs at the end of the queue, since nothing is lost before the deadline
choices.why: Everything is lost the day after it. Last in the queue is the place most likely to miss 1 September.

prompt: A new tech lead proposes "the standard 20% for engineering investment" for a team whose code costs it a large part of every sprint in interest, calling it the industry rule. What do both lessons say about the number?
hint: Technical Strategy: Debt, Budget and Build versus Buy, lesson 18; Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 12.

choices.text: Size the share to the interest the debt charges, and lower it as that falls
choices.why: Twenty percent is a common starting point that no evidence makes special, and one fifth was Coreto's choice. A team paying heavy interest needs more.

choices.text: Use it: twenty percent is the share the evidence supports
choices.why: The management course's lesson on prioritisation says the opposite: a common starting point, with nothing special about it.

choices.text: Drop the share and weigh each debt item against features
choices.why: One at a time, the comparison is built to make the debt lose. A share and a weighed backlog work together.

choices.text: Use it, and have product approve each item that goes inside
choices.why: Inside the share engineering chooses. Product sees the list and may question it, without approving item by item.

prompt: In June, Otávio and Davi agree to take the 10% cut, 6.6 engineer-years, by freezing 6.6 open roles from 1 July. By the lesson's arithmetic, what will the year's books show?
hint: Technical Strategy: Debt, Budget and Build versus Buy, lesson 11.

choices.text: The full cut, as long as the roles stay frozen into next year
choices.why: A budget is for a year. Months frozen next year count towards next year's books, not this one's.

choices.text: About half the cut: 6.6 engineer-years from July takes 13.2 roles
choices.why: A freeze from July saves half a year of each role. That is how a 10% cut agreed in a meeting becomes 5% on the books and a second round.

choices.text: The full cut, since the open roles are never filled this year
choices.why: Each role left empty from July saves six months of R$ 264,000, not twelve.

choices.text: Nothing saved, because open roles were never in the budget
choices.why: Open roles sit on the people line; leaving them unfilled is one of the three ways a cut lands there.

prompt: Six developers each lose about half an hour a day re-running a flaky suite, in ten-day sprints. Price the interest per sprint the way the management course does, then turn it into a year the way the strategy course's sheet does: 26 sprints at R$ 150 an engineer-hour. What is the interest a year, in R$?
hint: Technical Strategy: Debt, Budget and Build versus Buy, lesson 5; Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 14.

prompt: A team prices a hosted log service over three years with the lesson's four lines. Licence: R$ 6,000 a month. Integration: 200 hours. Operation: a tenth of an engineer every year, at R$ 264,000 an engineer-year. Exit: 150 hours, plus one month of licence while both run. At R$ 150 an hour, what is the three-year TCO, in R$?
hint: Technical Strategy: Debt, Budget and Build versus Buy, lesson 9.

prompt: Three items compete for the same people, each with a steady cost of delay. A: R$ 20,000 a week, 5 weeks of work. B: R$ 9,000 a week, 1 week. C: R$ 30,000 a week, 10 weeks. Done one at a time in CD3 order, what does the order cost in delay altogether, in R$?
hint: Technical Strategy: Debt, Budget and Build versus Buy, lesson 13.

prompt: For its quarterly review, a delivery company wants one cloud number with its before beside it. The bill goes from R$ 150,000 a month to R$ 168,000, while orders go from 300,000 a month to 400,000. Using the lesson's unit cost, by how many percent does the cloud cost per order fall?
hint: Technical Strategy: Debt, Budget and Build versus Buy, lesson 12; Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 19.

prompt: Coreto's new reservation service carries 90% of the traffic at the end of month 8. In the lesson, a strangler migration is measured not by its share of traffic but by how much of the old code is ___.
hint: Technical Strategy: Debt, Budget and Build versus Buy, lesson 7.

prompt: Coreto keeps one fifth of every sprint for engineering investment. The strategy course says that split is about who decides; the subject the delivery course sets beside it, ___, is about how much capacity there is to decide over.
hint: Technical Strategy: Debt, Budget and Build versus Buy, lesson 18; Delivery and Metrics: Flow, DORA and Incidents, lesson 12.

prompt: Put the usual cloud savings in the order the lesson works through them, first to last.
hint: Technical Strategy: Debt, Budget and Build versus Buy, lesson 12.
items: Switch off idle resources
Rightsize machines to their real load
Commit to a year of steady capacity
Change how a service is built
trap: Committing to capacity before removing the idle machines signs a contract for the waste, and rightsizing first tunes machines that should not exist. Architecture comes last because its saving has to beat a large cost in engineering hours.

prompt: Put the four steps that would have stopped the deploy portal while it was still a proposal in the lesson's order.
hint: Technical Strategy: Debt, Budget and Build versus Buy, lesson 15.
items: Ask the people whose work it would change
Measure the pain they have today
Build the smallest thing that removes it
Write the kill date before it ships
trap: Building the small thing before counting the pain skips the arithmetic that can end the proposal for free, and a kill date written after launch is written by people already attached to the tool.

prompt: A logistics company lists what would make leaving its managed queue service expensive. Match each finding to the kind of lock-in the lesson names.
hint: Technical Strategy: Debt, Budget and Build versus Buy, lesson 10.

pairs.left: The export returns messages only in the vendor's own format
The vendor's client library is called directly from 140 places
A two-year minimum term, with a fee for leaving early
Two engineers are the only ones who understand its delivery model

prompt: Davi has to put a number on the interest of a debt in a payments module. Which of these does the strategy course use as a source for measuring that interest, as distinct from guessing it? Choose all that apply.
hint: Technical Strategy: Debt, Budget and Build versus Buy, lesson 5; Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 14.

choices.text: Lead times of changes in the module, against similar ones
choices.why: That difference, times the changes that touched the module, is the tax on changes, usually the largest part of interest.

choices.text: A meeting where the engineers say how much the module costs them
choices.why: The answers come back confident and are not a measurement: the loudest complaint wins. A guess becomes credible only once it is measured.

choices.text: Incident hours whose cause names the module, from the log
choices.why: Incident hours divided by the sprints the log covers are the easiest part of interest to count.

choices.text: A static-analysis tool's figure for the module, in days of remediation
choices.why: Such a tool counts the principal of whatever its rules detect, with no idea of the interest.

choices.text: Engineers tagging their own time for a few sprints, one label per debt
choices.why: Tagging during the work catches reruns and hand work that leave no trace in a pull request or the incident log.

choices.text: Sales lost on the day the module made a big on-sale fail
choices.why: Lost sales are the risk lesson 20 prices. Counting them as interest as well would count one failure twice.

prompt: Which of these decisions earn an architecture decision record, by both lessons? Choose all that apply.
hint: Technical Strategy: Debt, Budget and Build versus Buy, lesson 17; Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 14.

choices.text: Which database a new service stores its data in
choices.why: It is expensive to reverse, which is the first of the lesson's two tests.

choices.text: Upgrading a logging library to its next minor version
choices.why: Cheap to reverse and nobody will ask why. A record for it is the noise that stops a log being read.

choices.text: Keeping every client in one database until there are fifty
choices.why: A debt taken on deliberately belongs in a record that writes down its trigger for repayment, so it is paid when it falls due.

choices.text: The name given to a new module in the monolith
choices.why: A name can be changed in an afternoon and explains no trade-off.

choices.text: How long a seat hold lasts before it expires
choices.why: A product decision in disguise: in a year somebody will ask who agreed to it, and the context is where that answer lives.

choices.text: The test runner one team prefers for its own code
choices.why: A preference inside one team, cheap to change, with no reason anybody will need to recover.
